docs/CHANGELOG.md:25:- **AWS account display names link accounts to workgroups (2026-08-25)** — an AWS account mapping file already names the team that owns each account (`display_name` in the Cloud Custodian export, a `display_name` column in the CSV exports), and that name was being thrown away at the CLI boundary: `UserMappingCliService.parseFromJson` flattened each account to `{email, awsAccountId}` and the backend's `CSVUserMappingParser` treated the column as an ignorable extra. The rule now implemented in one place — `WorkgroupAccountLinkService` — is that an account whose display name is `DevOps-x` belongs to the workgroup **`aws-DevOps-x`**: matched **exactly** on `"aws-" + display_name`, case-insensitively via `WorkgroupRepository.findByNameIgnoreCase`, and **created** (root level, `createdBy` = the acting ADMIN) when it does not exist. Suffixed variants such as `aws-DevOps-x-rolegreen` are deliberately not matched — a fuzzy rule here would hand an unrelated workgroup's members access to an account's assets, since a link is unified-asset-access **rule #9** (`WorkgroupAwsAccount`), not bookkeeping. Reuse rather than reimplementation: creation goes through `WorkgroupService.createWorkgroup` and assignment through `WorkgroupAwsAccountService.add`, whose `actorId` became nullable (`createdBy` is already nullable since V206's ON DELETE SET NULL) so the automated path can record "no interactive actor" instead of inventing one. Two entry points, both ADMIN-only. **During an import**: `BulkUserMappingEntry` gained `displayName`, carried by CLI `manage-user-mappings import` (JSON and the optional CSV `display_name` column), REST `POST /api/user-mappings/bulk`, MCP `import_user_mappings` and REST `POST /api/import/upload-user-mappings-csv`; linking runs in `UserMappingBulkImportService.execute` **after** the mappings commit, the same ordering rule the notification and onboarding side effects already follow, and is wrapped so a linking failure is reported rather than costing an import that already persisted. **On demand**: the new correction path re-links from what is already stored, with no file involved — CLI `manage-user-mappings link-workgroups [--dry-run]`, REST `POST /api/user-mappings/link-workgroup-accounts`, MCP `link_workgroup_aws_accounts`. That is what makes the display name worth persisting: new `user_mapping.aws_account_name` (**V260**, nullable, not backfilled, indexed) is deliberately **not** part of `uk_user_mapping_composite`, because the name describes the account rather than the identity of the mapping — so a rename updates the row instead of forking a second one, and both import paths refresh the name on rows they skip as duplicates (without that, the correction path would be blind to every account whose mappings already existed). Edge cases are result rows, never exceptions, so one bad account cannot abort a 10,000-account import: a display name that cannot legally be a workgroup name (`Workgroup.name` allows letters, digits, spaces and hyphens, ≤100 chars including the prefix — so `Data_Platform.01` is refused) is an **error with nothing created**; an account already assigned is `alreadyLinked`, an idempotent no-op that never drives a non-zero exit status; a lost race on workgroup creation re-reads and links to the winner's row, and a lost race on assignment (`DuplicateAccountException`) also reads as `alreadyLinked`, the unique index being the arbiter; duplicate pairs are collapsed before any DB work; names over 255 characters are dropped rather than truncated (a truncated name resolves to a *different* workgroup) and the drop is reported in `errors[]`. When one account carries several names, the correction path uses the most recently updated mapping's — and deliberately leaves the assignment made under the old name in place, because removing one revokes a workgroup's access and a correction run must not do that unasked. Bounded at both ends (§A04): the stored-name scan is paged at the query (`findAwsAccountDisplayNames(Pageable)`, grouped so one account owned by 40 people is one row), `MAX_PAIRS` 20,000 per run and `links[]` capped at 500 with exact counters, and every cap sets `truncated` and logs — never a silent one. §A09: `CREATE_WORKGROUP_FOR_AWS_ACCOUNT` and `LINK_WORKGROUP_ACCOUNT` audit lines carry actor, target and outcome, and every display name reaching a log or an error message goes through `UserMappingService.sanitizeForMessage` (log forging). Fixed while registering the new tool: `list_/add_/remove_workgroup_aws_account` and the three `workgroup_ad_domain` tools were in `McpToolPermissions.LISTING` but **absent from `.CALLING`**, so `tools/call` denied them unconditionally — visible in `tools/list` yet uncallable, the same fail-closed shape as the earlier `add_requirement` and `export_requirements` gaps; a new test pins all seven in both tables and pins `link_workgroup_aws_accounts` to the same permission as `add_workgroup_aws_account`, since the effect is the same. Files with no display name link nothing and report nothing, so every existing Excel and plain-CSV import is byte-identical. Tests: `WorkgroupAccountLinkServiceTest` (19 cases covering the matrix above), `CSVUserMappingParserDisplayNameTest`, `UserMappingCliServiceDisplayNameTest` (including a CSV *without* the column, since commons-csv throws on `get()` for an unknown header), `LinkWorkgroupAwsAccountsToolTest`, plus new cases in `UserMappingBulkImportServiceTest`, `ImportUserMappingsToolTest` and `McpToolPermissionsTest`. Samples: `testdata/user-mappings/accounts-with-display-name.json` and `mappings-with-display-name.csv`, both covering match / create / shared-name / illegal-name in one file. `docs/AWS_ACCOUNT_WORKGROUP_LINKING.md`.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:27:- **Full `excepted` recompute chunked to stop multi-minute lock holds (2026-08-24)** — `VulnerabilityRepository.recomputeExceptedAll()` was a single `UPDATE vulnerability v JOIN asset a … SET v.excepted = CASE WHEN EXISTS(…)` **with no WHERE clause**. It took exclusive row locks on every `vulnerability` row (~1.8M in production) and, through its correlated subquery, read locks on `vulnerability_exception` — holding both for the entire 53–180s transaction. Every concurrent writer to either table then blocked until lock-wait-timeout: bulk exception delete/import, CrowdStrike imports, per-asset recomputes. `DeadlockRetry` absorbed the failure, which is exactly why it stayed hidden — but the *other* operation still paid the full timeout first, observed as ~40s per `delete_all_vulnerability_exceptions` in both E2E runs, contending with "Async full excepted recompute complete: 1824736 rows in 53481 ms". Fix: `AsyncExceptionRecompute.recomputeAllChunked` drives the recompute as bounded **keyset** chunks (`CHUNK_SIZE` 10,000) through the new `recomputeExceptedForIdRange(afterId, throughId)`, each in its own REQUIRES_NEW transaction with per-chunk `DeadlockRetry`. Lock hold per transaction drops from minutes to milliseconds, so competing writers interleave between chunks instead of queueing behind one lock set; a chunk that loses a race replays only its own id range instead of the whole statement. **Keyset, not fixed-width id stepping** — the CrowdStrike import is delete-then-insert per asset, so ids are sparse and `MAX(id)` runs far ahead of the row count, which would make blind stepping spend most iterations on empty ranges. The daily 03:00 `recomputeAllExceptedScheduled` now delegates to the same driver (its orphaned `selfProvider` removed), so the nightly pass stops reintroducing the hold. Chunking gives up atomicity, and that is argued rather than assumed: the operation is already `@Async`, its documented contract is already eventual ("rows stay visible until it lands", failures "non-fatal; standing sweeps will retry"), a mid-statement failure already left partial state, and readers evaluate `v.excepted = 0` per row without a cross-table snapshot — so no guarantee is lost, and a failure now leaves a converged *prefix* rather than nothing. `recomputeExceptedAll()` is retained for the two integration tests that need single-step determinism on a tiny table, documented as not-for-production. Tests: `AsyncExceptionRecomputeChunkingTest` (5 cases pinning the traversal — sparse ids covered exactly once, half-open boundaries abutting without re-processing, no single range spanning the table) plus a `ExceptedFlagSqlAgreementIntegrationTest` case asserting the chunked statement assigns exactly what the atomic one does against a real database, with every flag pre-flipped so a skipped row cannot coincidentally match. Closes the `recomputeAll` lock-hold item open since the 2026-07-20 DB-pool work. OWASP: A01 reviewed — both new native queries bind parameters and take only primary-key boundaries from the preceding keyset read, on `@Async`/`@Scheduled` paths unreachable from any request.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:29:- **Vulnerability SLA anchored to remediation availability (2026-08-24)** — `secman.vulnerability.use-patch-publication-date` now defaults to **true** (both `application.yml` and the `VulnerabilitySettings` data class, which had to be changed together — they disagreed, and a new `VulnerabilitySettingsDefaultTest` now pins both). Age is measured from when a **fix became available**, falling back to CrowdStrike detection age per row when no patch date is published. Rationale: detection age answers "how long have we known", which resets whenever a host is rebuilt or newly onboarded — a 2023 CVE on a month-old host read as a month old — while remediation age answers "how long could we have fixed this and did not" and does not reward re-imaging. This only became possible in the same change that made the field arrive at all: the CLI batch payload had been dropping `patchPublicationDate` entirely, so the flag was inert on the production import path, and the ad-hoc lookup path never populated the field either (its DTO construction set neither publication date, so "persist it on save" persisted null forever — both now use the shared `FalconTimestamps` extractors). Two consequences documented rather than discovered later: (1) **overdue counts jump** on the first import after the change, since a patch date is normally much earlier than the detection date, so expect an outsized notification run; (2) **it is a one-way door** — `first_seen_at` is preserved as `min(prior, new)` across re-imports (the property that stops a re-import resetting the SLA clock), so once an import writes the older patch date, setting the flag back to false does **not** restore the previous anchors. A genuine revert is `UPDATE vulnerability SET first_seen_at = NULL WHERE source = 'CROWDSTRIKE'` plus a full re-import with the flag off. `requirePatchPublicationDate` stays **false** and is pinned by test: despite the near-identical name it is a *filter*, not an anchor, and enabling it would drop every vulnerability with no published patch date — hiding risk rather than re-dating it. Nothing changes until the next import; existing rows keep their current anchors. `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix, `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md`.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:31:- **CrowdStrike date semantics: three dates untangled (2026-08-24)** — reported as "the import is wrong: a 2023 CVE cannot be only 226 days old". Investigation showed the arithmetic was right and the *meaning* was not, plus four real defects underneath. Falcon's `created_timestamp` is when Spotlight created that finding **on that host**, and it creates every finding against a package in one batch — so a host legitimately shows one identical age across dozens of CVEs. Confirmed on live data: `detectedAt` clusters (80 rows on one date, 60 on another) while the newly captured `cve.published_date` spreads across dozens. Also confirmed that a CVE's ID year is its *reservation* year — `CVE-2023-53178` in this estate has `published_date = 2025-09-15` — so "a 2023 CVE can't be 62 days old" was never a sound inference; the data to see that simply was not being captured. Fixes: (1) **`extractPatchPublicationDate` asked `cve.published_date` FIRST**, so the column named for a patch — and used as the SLA anchor when `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE=true` — usually held the CVE *disclosure* date, silently answering "how long since a fix existed?" with "how long since the CVE was published". Genuine remediation dates (`remediation.vendor_release_date`, `remediation.published_date`) now win; the CVE fields are kept as the **last** resort rather than removed, because `require-patch-publication-date` filters imports on this being non-null and narrowing it would have silently dropped rows — nothing that was non-null before becomes null. (2) **Timezone bug**: `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityService.parseDetectionTimestamp` (the ad-hoc lookup behind the reported screen) parsed `"2026-01-10T22:18:26Z"` by *stripping* the `Z` and handing the rest to `LocalDateTime.parse`, relabelling a UTC instant as system-local instead of converting it — a whole-day shift across midnight, since age is `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between`. There were **four** copies of Falcon date parsing, one correct; all now delegate to one new `FalconTimestamps`, which also returns **null rather than `now()`** for an absent/unreadable date (defaulting to now reads as "detected today" = zero days = never overdue, a security miss dressed as a formatting fallback). (3) **The high-volume CLI batch payload dropped every date**: `/api/crowdstrike/servers/import` hand-built a map of `cveId`/`severity`/`affectedProduct`/`daysOpen` only, so `patchPublicationDate` was always null on the main import path and `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE` could never take effect there at all. It now also sends `detectedAt` and both publication dates, and the backend prefers `detectedAt` over re-deriving `importTimestamp − daysOpen` — the same cross-clock, twice-truncated reconstruction shape as the 2026-08-21 reconcile incident (`daysOpen` is still sent, and the reconstruction retained, so an older CLI keeps working). (4) Saving from the ad-hoc lookup dropped `patch_publication_date` entirely. New `cve_published_date` column (V259, nullable, not backfilled — the import is delete-then-insert, so rows acquire it on the next run) surfaced on the lookup page as a **CVE Published** column, with "Days Open" renamed to **Detected (days)** and tooltipped as "not the age of the CVE". Tests: `CrowdStrikeTimestampParsingTest` (8 cases pinning the timezone contract and unknown-stays-null), `FalconDateExtractionTest` (6 cases pinning the preference order *and* the deliberate CVE fallback). Three unrelated pre-existing failures that had been red on `main` were also fixed to get a green build: `ResponseControllerAccessControlTest` (four `Cannot infer type for type parameter 'O'` — backend test sources did not compile at all), `InstalledProductListServiceTest` ×2 (mockk had no stub for a `countProductsByServer` call the service gained), and `VulnerabilityServicePreviewIntegrationTest` (reflection lookup missing the `includeInstallerFindings` parameter added by product classification). `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:33:- **EOL mails carry the affected-systems table (2026-08-24)** — both EOL mail paths now embed the same table the product drilldown page shows, rendered by one new `EolFindingTableRenderer`: System, Type, Cloud account, **Cloud instance**, AD domain, Version, Release cycle, End of support, Status (plus Component for the owner notification, which spans many products; the broadcast is one product, so that column would be a constant). Previously the "Contact affected owners" broadcast (`/vulnerabilities/eol/products/{product}`) sent only the admin's free-text message with **no findings data at all**, and `secman send-eol-notifications` sent a 4-column Component/Version/Cycle/EOL table with no account, instance, domain, type or status — a recipient mapped to a whole AWS account could not tell which system or which account a row belonged to. Pieces: (1) **`cloudInstanceId` denormalized onto `eol_finding`** (V258, nullable, populated by `EolScanService` at both `ASSET_*` insertion sites exactly as `assetName`/`cloudAccountId`/`assetOwner` already are) and surfaced on `EolFindingResponse`, the page table and the CSV export so page, CSV and mail agree; deliberately **not backfilled** — the scan is delete-then-insert, so existing rows acquire it on the next `eol-sync` and read `-` until then; (2) **per-recipient scoping of the broadcast** — `EolBroadcastRecipientResolver.resolve` now returns `EolBroadcastRecipient(user, assetIds)` instead of `List<User>`, carrying the asset ids that made each user a recipient, and `EmailBroadcastService` renders only those rows into that recipient's copy. That linkage (owner, manual creator, scan uploader, AWS-account mapping, AD-domain mapping) is criteria 3/4/5/6/8 of §Unified Asset Access, hence provably a subset of what the recipient may already see (§A01) at **zero extra access queries** and with no way to drift from the rule that produced the recipient; sending one shared table would have disclosed other tenants' hostnames and account ids to every owner on the list. Manually-entered Cc addresses ride along on the owner's message and see that owner's rows only; (3) **bounded output** — rows and count are both taken at the query (`findByComponentNameForAssets` page of 200 + `countByComponentNameForAssets`), never fetched whole and sliced in Kotlin (§A04), and the remainder is disclosed in the table footer rather than silently truncated; (4) **one escaping sink** — the renderer escapes at assembly and strips CR/LF from the text part, replacing `EolNotificationService`'s private `escapeHtml`/`sanitizeForText` (which also escaped *before* truncating, so a 512-char cut could split an entity); the table is generated server-side at send time and never passes `EmailBroadcastService.sanitizeBroadcastHtml`, whose safelist strips every attribute except `a[href|title]` and would have removed the inline styles mail clients need. The compose modal now says the table is appended automatically and is scoped per recipient. Unrelated pre-existing breakage fixed to reach a green build: `ResponseControllerAccessControlTest` failed to compile on `main` (four `Cannot infer type for type parameter 'O'` on single-arg `exchange(...)`), so backend test sources did not build at all. `docs/EOL.md` §5.1.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:35:- **CrowdStrike morning over-deletion fixes (2026-08-21 incident: 727,637 rows)** — every morning the post-import reconcile sweep deleted far too many vulnerability rows. Root cause from the prod log: the CLI's cutoff arrived timezone-skewed (>1h in the backend's future), the old guard fell back to `backendNow − 30min`, and because the import ran longer than 30 minutes the sweep judged everything the run imported in its first half-hour "stale" and deleted it — 727,637 rows in one statement, aborted=false. Fixes, layered: (1) **cutoff translation** — the CLI now sends `clientNow`; the backend measures the clock offset and translates `importStartedAt` into its own clock, and without `clientNow` a future cutoff **aborts** the sweep (delete nothing) instead of guessing; (2) **failure-aware sweep scope** — hosts whose Falcon Stage-2 batch failed/was truncated (`StreamingImportResult.failedHosts`) or whose backend POST/per-server transaction failed (`BatchStorageResult.failedHostnames`, `ImportStatisticsDto.failedHostnames`) are excluded from `queriedHosts`, since their un-refreshed rows were never fetched, not remediated; (3) **percentage brake** `CROWDSTRIKE_RECONCILE_MAX_DELETE_PERCENT` (default 20, 100 disables) over the resolved scope, fail-CLOSED on count errors — the zero-refresh brake only catches fully-empty runs; (4) **scoped per-host replace** — `importVulnerabilitiesForServer` no longer wipes every row on the asset: it deletes `source=CROWDSTRIKE` rows at the batch's `runSeverities` (new optional DTO field; source-only fallback for old callers), so MEDIUM/LOW and XLSX/nmap/manual rows survive, and a batch whose rows are ALL filtered out (blank CVE / missing patch date) skips the delete instead of committing delete-without-reinsert; (5) **stale-asset cleanup correctness** — rule A now vetoes assets with a recent `crowdStrikeAgentSeenAt` (a fully-patched host with a live sensor never refreshes `crowdStrikeLastImportedAt`), brake numerator and deletion use one shared cutoff and the same query, and the brake fails closed when the tracked-asset count is unavailable; (6) **observability** — reconcile audit columns on `crowdstrike_reconcile_job` (V257: queried/resolved/excluded counts, stale candidates, refreshed, dry_run), `--reconcile-dry-run` CLI flag, per-host replace logging at INFO, a `CROWDSTRIKE_RECONCILE_ABORTED` chat-notification event, and the MV refresh `triggered_by` insert no longer dies on over-length reasons (`.take(50)`, the log's second error). `scripts/import.sh` `--last-seen-days` regression 1→30 fixed (comment already said 30). `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md` §CrowdStrike reconcile sweep.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:36:- **Apple `container` database selection (`--db`)** — `secman-container.sh up` now takes `--db container|host|none` (plus `--db-host/--db-port/--db-name`; `--with-db`/`--no-db` are aliases for the first and last). `container`, the default, runs the in-container MariaDB and publishes it on :3306; `host` runs none and points the stack at the MariaDB already installed on the Mac; `none` leaves `DB_CONNECT` to `pass-cli`. `host` was previously not reachable at all: the egress policy carries only 80/443/22 to allow-set addresses, so port 3306 to the Mac was refused with no rule capable of permitting it. The entrypoint now settles the mode **before** the firewall is built, resolves the Mac's address (it is the container's default gateway, which only the container can see), and writes the result to `/run/secman-dev/db/env` — the single file the firewall, `devctl` and every login shell read, so the iptables rule and the JDBC URL cannot disagree, including after a `refresh-egress` that inherits none of the entrypoint's environment. The rule is deliberately narrow: one address, one port, outside the allow-set (which is only ever matched on 80/443/22), and the address must be private — a public one is refused unless `SECMAN_DEV_DB_ALLOW_PUBLIC=1`, so a convenience flag cannot become general 3306 egress. The choice is made effective rather than advisory: `/etc/profile.d/secman-dev.sh` exports the resulting `DB_CONNECT` (plus the throwaway `DB_USERNAME`/`DB_PASSWORD` in `container` mode only), and `scripts/startbackenddev.sh` now honours a preset `DB_CONNECT` and falls back to `pass://Test/SECMAN/DB_CONNECT` when it is unset — unchanged behaviour on a Mac. `devctl db status` / `secman-container.sh db` report the mode, the URL and a live reachability probe, and name the three silent failure modes of `--db host` in order (server not running, bound to 127.0.0.1 only, no grant for the container's subnet); `devctl db start` refuses outside `container` mode rather than raising a second server behind a URL that names a different one. Every value that reaches an iptables rule or a JDBC URL goes through a closed character allowlist at both ends (§A03). `docs/APPLE_CONTAINER_DEV.md` §Choosing the database.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:38:- **Apple `container` shielded dev environment (macOS/Apple silicon)** — `./scripts/container/secman-container.sh` builds and drives one long-lived Apple `container` VM that carries the whole toolchain (Temurin 25, Gradle 9.7.0, Node 24, Go 1.24, uv/Python 3.13, MariaDB 11.4, nginx) plus Claude Code, Kimi CLI and `pass-cli`, so the agents run inside a shield rather than on the developer's Mac. Three properties are the point. **One host path**: the source tree passed with `--src` is the only bind mount; the Gradle/npm caches, the agent state, the Proton Pass session and the MariaDB data directory live in named volumes — invisible to macOS, faster than virtiofs, and no widening of the exposure the container exists to narrow. `up` refuses `/`, `/Users`, `$HOME` and friends rather than trusting the caller to notice. **Egress by iptables alone, deliberately without a proxy**: `OUTPUT` policy `DROP`, and the only ways out are loopback, replies on established connections, DNS to the resolvers in `/etc/resolv.conf`, and TCP on 80/443/22 to an address in the allow-set. That set is built from the allowlist's hostnames resolved to their A records, its address/CIDR literals, and GitHub's published ranges from `api.github.com/meta` (a service across that many prefixes cannot be covered by resolving a few names); it is held in an `ipset` where the kernel has one — a single hash lookup per packet and an atomic swap on refresh — and in a plain rule chain where it does not, both probed rather than assumed because Apple's kernel is trimmed. The consequence is stated rather than buried: filtering is by **address, not name**, so anything else answering on an allowlisted address is reachable, and an address that rotates out of DNS stays permitted until the next refresh while its replacement is not. The second half is handled by re-resolving every 30 minutes (`SECMAN_EGRESS_REFRESH_MINUTES`), without which a container left running overnight starts failing npm and Maven downloads for reasons that look nothing like a firewall; the first half is inherent to packet-layer filtering. Denials `REJECT` rather than `DROP` so a blocked tool fails immediately instead of hanging, and a rate-limited `LOG` rule plus the reject counter are the record of what was refused now that there is no proxy log. Three guards fail closed: the container **refuses to start** if a non-allowlisted host is reachable, an allowlist that renders to nothing is refused, and a resolution round in which more than half the names fail is refused as broken DNS rather than installed as a policy that reaches almost nothing. The allowlist covers both agents, Proton, GitHub, Gradle/Maven/Google/JetBrains/Adoptium, npm, Go, PyPI, Playwright, Debian/MariaDB apt, and the hosts the app itself calls (`endoflife.date`, `api.crowdstrike.com` and its regional siblings, `openrouter.ai`, `hooks.slack.com`, `api.telegram.org`, `acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org`); `SECMAN_HOST` and AWS's regional endpoints are deliberately absent, since neither can be guessed. **Ports 8080/4321/443/3306** come back to the Mac, with nginx terminating TLS on 443 in front of both services because the `secman_auth` cookie is `Secure` and a plain-HTTP dev origin produces a login that silently never persists. Apple-specific behaviour is handled rather than documented-around: the default kernel has no working nftables, so `iptables-legacy` is pinned explicitly (a silent fall-through to the nft backend would fail *open*); IPv6 is incomplete, so it is disabled and all `ip6tables` policies set to `DROP`; there is no privileged mode, so exactly `NET_ADMIN` + `NET_RAW` are added; `--publish` needs macOS 26 and the script says so on 15; options must precede the image name; macOS reserves ports below 1024 for root, so `up` probes and falls back to publishing `:443` on `8443`; virtiofs presents the Mac's uid (501, not 1000), so the entrypoint creates `dev` with the uid/gid that actually own `/workspace`. Because there is no proxy, nothing in the container needs `HTTP_PROXY` or `-Dhttps.proxyHost` — no JVM banner on every start, and no tool that quietly ignores those variables and behaves differently from the rest. `pass-cli` uses `PROTON_PASS_KEY_PROVIDER=file` (there is no OS keyring in the VM) with the session on a named volume, so `pass-cli login --interactive` is a one-time step and no Proton state ever touches the Mac's filesystem or Keychain. The `dev` user has no sudo: the firewall and its allowlist are root-owned, so an agent session cannot dismantle the shield it runs in. Values that reach SQL identifiers or an OpenSSL subject go through a closed character allowlist first (§A03), and `--allow-domain` entries clear a strict hostname/CIDR regex before they can reach an `iptables -d` argument. Full reference: `docs/APPLE_CONTAINER_DEV.md`.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:40:- **Vulnerability export IP addresses** — the Excel export has carried an `IP` column all along (`ExportJobService.createHeaderRow`, column 1, fed from `Asset.ip`), but it came out blank for CrowdStrike-imported assets because the ingest side never asked CrowdStrike for the IP. Spotlight returns `local_ip` — together with `machine_domain`, `instance_id`, `service_provider_account_id` and `os_version` — inside a `host_info` object that is omitted from the response unless `facet=host_info` is requested, and all four Spotlight vulnerability queries (`CrowdStrikeApiClientImpl.queryAllVulnerabilitiesBulk`, `queryBatchVulnerabilities`, `querySpotlightApi`, and the backend's `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityService.queryCrowdStrikeApi`) asked only for `facet=cve`. Every mapper already read those fields off `host_info`, so the missing facet NULLed the asset IP silently instead of failing — the same failure mode as the Discover `facet=install_usage` gap fixed earlier. Second, narrower loss: the per-host batch took `firstVuln?.ip`, so an IP present on any row but the first was dropped; a shared `List<CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityDto>.resolveHostIp()` now takes the first non-blank IP across the host's rows (`ServersCommand` ×2, `QueryCommand`), mirroring how `cloudInstanceId`/`osVersion` were already resolved, and the live-lookup transient asset in `CrowdStrikeQueryService` does the same so IP-scoped exceptions keep matching. `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityImportService.updateAsset` already writes a changed non-blank IP onto an existing asset, so existing rows fill in on the next import rather than needing a backfill. No export-side change was needed or made — the column, the DTO field and the writer were all correct.

docs/CHANGELOG.md:46:- **Public standard download: any standard, any release, over a plain GET** — the unauthenticated `/requirements/download` page could export the whole corpus or one use case, but not a *standard*, and there was no way to ask for "the latest released version of the IT/OT Security standard" from a script. `GET /api/requirements/export/{docx,xlsx}` now take four optional query parameters — `standard` (exact name, case-insensitive), `standardId` (wins if both given), `release` (`latest`, or an exact version) and the pre-existing `releaseId` — all `IS_ANONYMOUS`, matching the four public export endpoints that already existed. A standard has **no direct link to requirements**: `Standard.useCases` joins `Requirement.usecases`, so a standard selects every requirement tagged with any of its use cases, de-duplicated and ordered by chapter — the same rule `StandardController.getStandardRequirements` applies. Release-scoped standard exports filter `RequirementSnapshot.usecaseIdsSnapshot` through `ReleaseRequirementScopeService`, so a historical download is reproducible rather than re-derived from live rows. Three failure modes fail loudly rather than degrading: `release=latest` with **no ACTIVE release** is a 404 and never silently serves the live corpus ("the latest release" and "whatever is in the editor" are different answers); `releaseId` and `release` identifying different releases is a 400 rather than one silently winning; and a standard with **no use cases mapped** returns `{"message": "No requirements found for this standard"}` rather than falling through to everything, so a half-configured standard cannot publish the full corpus by accident. Name matching is a bound-parameter `LOWER(s.name) = LOWER(:name)` fetch-join (`Standard.useCases` is LAZY, so a detached read would throw); an over-long name is rejected before the query runs. The standard name reaches `Content-Disposition`, so `StandardExportScopeService.exportFilename` strips it to `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, collapses repeated dots and drops a leading one — `IT/OT Security` becomes `ITOT_Security`, `../../etc/passwd` becomes `etcpasswd` — and the xlsx endpoint gained the `"`/CR/LF strip the docx path already had. A new slim `GET /api/standards/public` returns `{id, name}` only so the picker works logged out; `GET /api/standards` stays `IS_AUTHENTICATED`, keeping descriptions, use-case mappings and timestamps behind auth. The download page gains a third *Complete Standard* card that reuses the existing release selector (which already lists every release plus "Current Version (Live)") and shows the equivalent name-based URL for the current selection, so the page documents its own API. `RequirementExportScope.STANDARD` was added for the template usage audit. **Not rate limited** — public document generation was already an unauthenticated CPU cost before this change and stays a reverse-proxy concern. Tests: `StandardExportScopeServiceTest` (25 unit), `PublicStandardExportIntegrationTest` (15, every request credential-free, including that `GET /api/standards` still 401s), `requirementDownloadUrl.test.ts` (8). See `docs/PUBLIC_STANDARD_DOWNLOAD.md`.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:47:- **EOL matching for applications and frameworks: Java's nine distributions, the .NET family, and four rules that stop the estate being told supported software is dead** — the EOL dashboard showed operating systems only while `/products` plainly listed `.Net Framework 4.8` and `.NET Core 1.0`–`6.0`. The cause was not a missing data source: `EolSubjectType.ASSET_PRODUCT` and `scanInstalledProducts` already existed and were correct. `installed_product` was simply **empty at scan time** — it is fed by CrowdStrike **Discover** via the separate `secman installed-products` CLI, not by the Spotlight vulnerability import that fills `vulnerability.vulnerable_product_versions` behind `/products`. The first-ever Discover import landed 182,131 rows across 2,010 assets and the scan went from 304 findings to real coverage; **no new scan source was needed and none was added.** What *was* broken is matching, in four ways, each proven against the live inventory rather than inferred. **Java could not match at all**: endoflife.date publishes no generic `java` product — it publishes `oracle-jdk`, `amazon-corretto`, `eclipse-temurin`, `azul-zulu`, `microsoft-build-of-openjdk`, `redhat-build-of-openjdk`, `openjdk-builds-from-oracle`, `graalvm-ce` and `oracle-graalvm`, because Oracle JDK 8, Corretto 8 and Temurin 8 end on different dates — so the five curated aliases targeting `"java"` resolved to a key no product owned and were **dropped silently at index build time**, which is the documented behaviour for speculative targets and is exactly why the failure was invisible. Each spelling now maps to the distribution that ships it, an unidentifiable build produces no finding rather than borrowing another vendor's date, and where the name is ambiguous (`OpenJDK Platform 11`) the vendor decides — enabled by adding corporate suffixes (`Inc`, `Corporation`, `Ltd`, `GmbH`, `LLC`) to the noise tokens so `Oracle Corporation OpenJDK Platform` tokenizes to a usable alias prefix. **Legacy Java versions were unmatchable**: Java numbered releases `1.x` up to Java 8 and plainly `x` after, so `1.8.0.392` segments to `[1,8,0,392]` and prefix-matches no cycle; it is now rewritten to `8.0.392`, only for the Java distributions and only when the leading segment is exactly `1` (`1.4` → `4`, which no cycle carries, so it fails closed). **Labelled cycles matched by list order**: every `windows` cycle upstream carries an edition label (`10-1507`, `11-24h2-e-lts`) and cycle comparison keeps only the leading numeric run, so `10-1507` collapsed to `[10]` and the Windows Server 2022 build `10.0.20348.3451` prefix-matched it — **3,672 findings, 42 % of the total, reporting supported servers as end of life since 2017**, decided by nothing but release ordering. Labelled cycles are now skipped (`isNumericCycle`), because which edition a bare build number belongs to cannot be recovered without a build-to-release table the catalogue does not publish; Windows Server is unaffected, its cycles are plain numbers. **Distribution packages were judged against upstream lifecycles**: a packaging revision (`1.18.0-6ubuntu14.4`, `2026c-1.el8_10`, `3.4.1-11.amzn2`, `~esm1`) *proves* the support contract belongs to the distribution — Canonical still supports nginx 1.18 long after upstream dropped it — and a maintainer vendor (`Ubuntu Developers <ubuntu-devel-discuss@…>`) proves it even when the version looks plain, which is how the Ubuntu npm library `node-arrify 2.0.1-2` was reported as "Node.js 2, end of life". Both are rejected; Red Hat and Amazon Linux are deliberately **not** vendor-blocked because their packages carry `.el8`/`.amzn2` in the version and blocking the vendor would make `redhat-build-of-openjdk` unmatchable. Also curated: `Microsoft Windows Desktop Runtime - 8.0.21` is the .NET desktop runtime, and without an explicit entry the shorter `microsoft windows` alias captured it and reported **.NET 8 as Windows 8, EOL 2016**; and `ASP .Net Core` → `dotnet` (no product of its own upstream, its versions track .NET exactly), noting the alias is `asp net core` because tokenization strips the leading dot. Net effect on the live estate: 304 → **4,492 findings** (3,386 EOL, 1,106 approaching) with the Windows, Node-library and distro-package false-positive classes eliminated — Internet Explorer 11 (762), .NET 8 approaching (443), SQL Server 2016 (279), .NET 6 (165), Visual Studio 15.0/16.0/10.0, Splunk 8.1/9.0/9.2, and Oracle JDK 6/7/8/11 plus Corretto and Oracle's OpenJDK builds now reporting for the first time. Nine new matcher tests (EVM-015..023) pin every rule in both directions, including the exact Windows Server 2022 build number and the requirement that the OS path stay byte-identical; the 14 pre-existing cases still pass. **OWASP: A04 touched (matching correctness) — clean, 0 static findings**; the change is a pure function with no SQL, auth, I/O or HTML surface. Unrelated fix required to verify anything at all: `RequirementExportTemplateValidationServiceTest` referenced `org.apache.poi.xwpf.usermodel.HeaderFooterType`, which does not exist (it is `org.apache.poi.wp.usermodel`), and that single unresolved reference had been failing `compileTestKotlin` and therefore blocking the **entire** backend test suite since the requirement-export-template commit. With it fixed, `RequirementExportTemplateIntegrationTest.an uploaded template can be deactivated and activated again` failed — but on investigation the **endpoint is correct and the test was wrong**: `@MicronautTest` wraps each test in a transaction, so the injected repository holds one persistence context for the whole method while the controller commits in its own. The first `findById` is the initial load and reads the database; the second returns the **cached instance** and never sees the controller's write. Proven by instrumenting the assertion — the activate response body reported `ACTIVE` while the repository re-read reported `INACTIVE`. Fixed with the `entityManager.clear()` pattern already used by `StatisticsAggregateIntegrationTest` and `ExceptedFlagSqlAgreementIntegrationTest`, wrapped in a `rereadFromDb` helper whose KDoc records the trap: only the *second* read of an entity lies, so this failure mode reads exactly like a broken endpoint. Backend suite is green.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:48:- **Company Word template for requirement exports: real release metadata, an in-place insertion point, a seeded example** — the template machinery already existed (`RequirementExportTemplate`, `/api/requirement-export-templates`, `templateMode=LATEST` already the export default) but nothing ever produced a templated document: no example shipped and nothing seeded one, so `LATEST` found no ACTIVE row and silently degraded to the built-in layout. Three things were wrong underneath. **Release metadata was faked** — `releaseVersion` was sliced out of the document title with `title.substringAfter("Release ")` and `releaseStatus` was hard-coded to `""`, so a cover page could never carry either; the `Release` entity is now threaded through `resolveRequirementExportData` → `exportWordDocument` → `createTemplatedWordDocument` and binds `${releaseName}`, `${releaseVersion}`, `${releaseDate}` (falling back to `createdAt`), `${releaseStatus}` and `${releaseDescription}` for real, with `${useCaseName}` from the `UseCase` entity. All resolve to `""` for a live (non-release) export — the same contract, told honestly. **`${requirements}` was not an insertion point** — it was replaced with an empty string and content always appended after a page break, so a template could not put a cover page before and an appendix after; it is now an anchor, with `appendRequirementContent` taking a paragraph factory and the templated path inserting via `XmlCursor` in front of the marker (a fresh cursor per insert, because POI invalidates it) before removing the marker paragraph. That removal indexes into `document.bodyElements`, **not** `getPosOfParagraph` — the latter counts paragraphs only, so on a template containing a table (a cover page usually does) the two disagree and the wrong element is deleted. Absent marker still falls back to appending, which is what `MissingPlaceholderBehavior.APPEND` means. **A marker in a table cell, header or footer cannot host body-level content**, so validation now rejects it in strict mode and warns in append mode rather than producing a silently wrong document.
