docs/CHANGELOG.md:50:- **AWS account onboarding: welcome mail, direct and guided risk assessments** — the "new AWS account discovered → mail the owner and start an assessment" path becomes a three-mode capability, and the scoping decision moves to the person who actually knows. `WELCOME_ONLY` sends a welcome mail from a classpath template; `DIRECT` additionally starts an assessment for a use case the operator names (today's behaviour); `GUIDED` mails the owner a **one-time, expiring link** whose answers resolve through admin-configured rules into a *set* of use cases, and creates the assessment only on submit, scoped to the **union** of every matching rule. All three run from CLI (`--onboarding-mode`, `--welcome-email`, `--questionnaire-expiry-days` on `import` and `import-s3`), REST and MCP, all dry-runnable, plus a first-class `simulate-onboarding` verb (CLI + REST + MCP `simulate_account_onboarding`) that runs the whole path against a made-up account id and address — the *same* code path a real import runs, not a mock, which is what makes it a rehearsal and why it is rate limited, audited, and stamps every simulated mail with "this is a test, sent by <actor>". **The backward-compatibility contract is the load-bearing part**: a caller sending only `startRiskAssessment=true` — every `extensions/` client, `import-s3`, both existing E2E drivers — resolves to `DIRECT` **with no welcome mail**, byte-identical to before, reconciled in one function (`AccountOnboardingMode.resolve`); an explicit non-`DIRECT` mode combined with that flag is rejected, never guessed. **The matcher never decides**: it sees only choice ids (a BOOLEAN question is two choices, no second code path), every matching active rule contributes and nothing wins, `priorityOrder` is display order only, the single `isDefault` rule is consulted **after** everything else fails, and a resolution producing no requirements in the ACTIVE release is an error rather than an empty questionnaire. Answers that match nothing are **persisted** and the invite stays usable, so an admin can add the missing rule and the owner's original link still works. Rules are normalized tables, not a `ruleJson` blob (`DemandClassificationRule`'s precedent exists for a recursive condition; this one is a flat AND over choice ids, and the rule→use-case link needs real FK integrity). **The public questionnaire is the first genuinely unauthenticated write path in the codebase** and is treated as such: 256-bit `SecureRandom` token (not `UUID.randomUUID()`, because this token *creates* an assessment), single use enforced by a guarded UPDATE **claimed before** creation, 14-day expiry, a byte-identical 404 for malformed/unknown/expired/used/cancelled so the endpoint is no enumeration oracle, the account id **masked** to four digits and the owner email never returned, a new bounded fixed-window rate limiter with a dedicated failed-lookup bucket, `@Secured(IS_ANONYMOUS)` explicit on every method plus an `intercept-url-map` entry so a stale `secman_auth` cookie cannot 401 an owner out of their own link, and the full token never logged, never returned by any API, never printed by the CLI, never in an MCP result and never minted by a dry run — all asserted. Unanswered invites get one reminder then lapse; **nothing is ever auto-created**, because an assessment scoped by a guess looks authoritative and is not. `createAssessment` now takes `useCases: Set<UseCase>` (`use_case_name` widened 255→1024 in V253) and `sendStartNotification` was promoted to `notifyAssessmentStarted` so the guided path reuses the identical mail. Five private helpers were extracted from `AwsAccountRiskAssessmentService` into `EmailTemplateRenderer` — with a **closed template allowlist**, because the basenames are operator config and interpolating one into `getResourceAsStream` would be a classpath-traversal read — and the twice-copied recipient regex into `EmailAddressValidator`. New: ADMIN-**or-SECCHAMPION** admin API and UI (a deliberate widening vs Demand Classification's read-both/write-ADMIN, with a coverage matrix that shows which answer combinations would dead-end *before* an owner hits one), `/onboarding/[token]` public page, `docs/ACCOUNT_ONBOARDING.md` with 28 worked examples covering every mode × dry-run × surface, and the `/account-onboarding` skill in both trees. **OWASP: A01/A02/A03/A04/A05/A07/A08/A09 touched — 0 BLOCK.** **The Kotlin and CLI halves are compile-unverified**: the session had Java 21 only, no Gradle 9.7.0 distribution (services.gradle.org 403s through the agent proxy) and no Maven Central route. The frontend is fully verified — `npm ci`, `npm run build` and 149 unit tests green — as are the skill-sync gate and the driver's bash syntax.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:51:- **End-of-life lifecycle management: a catalogue, a matcher that refuses to guess, owner mail and a top-10 repository ranking** — secman gains a full EOL feature: `secman eol-sync` pulls a lifecycle catalogue and re-matches every system's OS and installed products plus every imported GitHub repository's dependencies against it; `secman send-eol-notifications` mails account owners about software going EOL in the next 12 months; `/vulnerabilities/eol` answers "which software in my account / on my servers is end of life"; and ADMIN/SECCHAMPION get the top 10 repositories by distinct EOL components. **Source: endoflife.date** — public, unauthenticated, ~350 products covering both halves of this inventory (Windows/Windows Server, RHEL, Ubuntu, Debian, SLES, Amazon Linux, ESXi, Java, .NET, Python, Node.js, nginx, Apache, Tomcat, PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Spring Boot, Kubernetes). Microsoft's Lifecycle API was considered and rejected *as a replacement* (Microsoft-only, needs an Entra app) but is a sensible future second `sourceKey` — `EolProduct` is keyed `(source_key, product_key)` for exactly that. **The fetch runs in the backend, not the CLI**, same shape as `import-github-repos`: the host allowlist, the SSRF checks and the audit record stay in one place and the CLI host needs no egress. **The matcher never guesses** — a component whose version cannot be parsed, or whose version matches no cycle, produces no finding, because a false "end of life" on a production server lands on an owner's remediation list and costs more than a miss. Two consequences it took real care to get right: a version embedded in the name beats the version field (Windows Server reports build `10.0.17763`, which matches no cycle; the `2019` in the name does), and a cycle upstream flags EOL *without a date* is EOL with a **null** horizon, never a zero-day countdown — the owner mail promises "within N months" and must not put undated cycles in that window. Cycle resolution compares whole dot-segments, so `4.10` never matches cycle `4.1`. **Repository components are a deliberate under-approximation**: a Dependabot alert names the vulnerable *range*, never the resolved version, so the scan takes the range's upper bound — from `< 4.17.21` it knows the dependency is below 4.17.21, hence if the cycle containing 4.17.21 is already EOL then whatever is installed is in that cycle or older and is EOL too. Only `EOL` is recorded there ("approaching" says nothing about the older version in use) and an unparseable range is skipped. Findings are **replace-per-run** by `scan_run_id` with an explicit delete — `Asset` owns no cascade to `EolFinding`, because mixing cascade with manual delete-insert is what dropped 166,812 rows to 1,819 in the CrowdStrike import. Only EOL and approaching-EOL rows are stored; persisting supported ones would be a row per product per asset. **Every asset-scoped read resolves accessible asset ids first and binds them as an `IN` list**; `EolFindingRepository` has no unscoped find-all on a user-facing path, the repository ranking is ADMIN/SECCHAMPION only mirroring `GithubRepositoryController`, and an out-of-scope asset id answers 404 identically to a nonexistent one. Recipient resolution reuses `AwsAccountRecipientResolver` rather than inventing an ownership model, and addresses are rejected rather than repaired (the value is an SMTP recipient, a stored result and a log line — three sinks from one string). New: `src/backendng/…/domain/Eol*`, `EolCatalogClient/CatalogSyncService/VersionMatcher/ScanService/QueryService/NotificationService/AdminService/Writer`, `EolController`, CLI `eol-sync` + `send-eol-notifications`, `/vulnerabilities/eol`, a Lifecycle badge on `/installed-products`, `docs/EOL.md`, and the `/e2eeol` skill. **OWASP: A01/A03/A04/A05/A08/A09/A10 touched — 0 BLOCK, 35 REVIEW, all reviewed** (26 A01-sql-authz on catalogue reference-data reads and on scoped reads that take a bound `assetIds` list; 6 A03-shell-sh on quoted `curl` argv in the E2E driver; 1 A04-todo-auth on the controller's `IS_AUTHENTICATED` default, deliberate because the reads are asset-scoped and the admin verbs carry their own `@Secured`; 1 A10-outbound inside the test that asserts the SSRF guard). **Kotlin is compile-unverified** — no Gradle distribution and no Maven Central route in that session; the frontend `npm ci && npm run build` gate and the 99-test frontend unit tier are green, as is `check-skill-sync.sh`.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:53:- **Zero-trust mobile relay: a DMZ server, secman's RBAC mirrored onto it, and an iOS app** — secman gains an outbound-only publisher (`SECMAN_RELAY_ENABLED=true`, off by default) that pushes an admin-level status snapshot to a standalone Go relay in a DMZ; the relay serves it read-only to iPhone/iPad clients and **can never reach back**. Direction is the whole design: secman dials out, the relay holds no secman credential and is never told where secman is, so a fully compromised DMZ box discloses dashboard aggregates and nothing else — no database, no write path, no lateral move. That is why a reverse proxy was rejected: a proxy needs an inbound path *and* a credential inside the DMZ. **Authorization is secman's, mirrored, not reinvented**: every snapshot section carries the roles its originating controller demands (`DashboardController`'s `@Secured("ADMIN","SECCHAMPION")` → `requiredRoles` on `kpis`), secman pushes each user's live roles as a principal record, and a read needs a matching role **and** a device scope naming the section — a scope narrows, never widens. Roles are resolved from the principal on every request and never cached on the device or baked into a token, so a demotion bites on the very next request with nothing to invalidate; principals are replace-on-push so roles can shrink, revocations stay additive so one is never undone by omission, and out-of-role / out-of-scope / nonexistent all answer an identical 403. **Sign-in layers three separate proofs**: Apple and Google ID tokens verified against their JWKS (RS256 pinned, iss/aud/exp and a single-use relay-issued nonce all checked — `aud` is what stops a token minted for another app); GitHub via the relay as a confidential OAuth client so the app never holds a GitHub credential; and a Secure Enclave P-256 key proving the device on every request. Verifying an identity grants nothing on its own — only the principal list secman pushed does. **Admins are held to a stronger bar**: a privileged role can only be bound via Apple or Google, re-checked on *every* token issue so a promotion invalidates a weakly-bound device, and the relay refuses to boot if a privileged role has no reachable strong provider. Binding is proof-of-possession throughout: the login nonce is bound to the device key and the binding request must carry that key's signature, so a captured ID token cannot register someone else's key. TLS on a selectable port in three modes — a **stdlib RFC 8555 ACME client** (Let's Encrypt, HTTP-01, renewal at 30 days), a file pair hot-reloaded on change, or plaintext for ALB termination behind an explicit `RELAY_PLAINTEXT_ACK=true`. The relay is **zero-third-party-dependency by contract** (its supply chain is the Go release plus this repo, and `go build` needs no module proxy), snapshot state is memory-only, and it fails closed on weak or placeholder secrets exactly as `JwtSigningValidator` does. 189 Go tests including a mock ACME CA that signs a real CSR and verifies every JWS, a mock OIDC issuer covering algorithm confusion / audience / issuer / expiry / nonce replay / key rotation, and end-to-end RBAC, revocation and staleness cases; a shared known-answer vector pins the ingest signature across Kotlin and Go so the two cannot drift silently. New: `src/relay/`, `com.secman.relay`, `RelayIdentity` entity, ADMIN-only `/api/relay/*`, `docs/RELAY.md`, and `extensions/secman_app_ios` (SwiftUI, iOS 26+, no third-party packages). **OWASP: A01/A02/A03/A04/A05/A07/A09/A10 touched — two A02 BLOCKs remain by design** (`RelayDigest` — SHA-256 as a message digest and over a 100-bit single-use token; BCrypt is the wrong tool there and would turn an O(1) lookup into an O(n) scan of a slow function on an unauthenticated endpoint), A10 reviewed: the outbound URL is operator config no request can influence. **The Kotlin and Swift halves are compile-unverified** — Maven Central was blocked by the egress policy, only JDK 21 was present, and there is no Swift toolchain.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:54:- **`/secure-code` — OWASP Top 10 by construction, with a static gate that is actually tested** — `CLAUDE.md` §"OWASP Top 10 Compliance" was already binding and already good, but it is ~60 bullet points across ten categories, which is more than anyone holds in working memory while writing a controller. The predictable failure is not defiance but **partial recall**: you remember `@Secured` and forget the path id is untrusted; you bind `:name` and forget `ExcelSanitizer` on the export three files over. The new skill closes that gap in three phases. **Phase 1 routes before writing**: a 17-row table maps "does this change accept a client id / write a query / render HTML / take an upload / parse XML / make an outbound call / …" to the two or three A01–A10 categories it can actually violate and, for each, the *one existing control to reuse* — so ten categories collapse to the three that apply, and the answer is a function to call rather than a principle to remember. **Phase 2 writes with that control** (`references/controls.md`: the canonical snippet plus the file that already does it correctly, for all ten categories — `AssetFilterService`, `McpToolGuards`, bound-`:param` queries with a closed allowlist for non-bindables, `DOMPurify` at the assignment site, `ExcelSanitizer`, `ImportController.validateFile`, the `NmapParserService` XXE block, `BCryptPasswordEncoder`, `EncryptedStringConverter`, `SlackClient.validateWebhookUrl`), under three rules: reuse never re-implement, never work around a control to make something build/start/pass, deny by default. **Phase 3 verifies three ways** — the static gate, a semantic re-read against `references/blind-spots.md`, and `/security-review` when the diff touches auth, crypto, upload, export or outbound HTTP — closing with the one-line `OWASP: … touched — clean` verdict the review gate already required. **The gate is `./scripts/owasp-check.sh`**, 27 rules across A01–A10, and its design is mostly a set of decisions about *not* crying wolf. It is **diff-scoped by default** (merge-base with `origin/main`, working tree and **untracked files** included — a freshly generated controller is invisible to `git diff` and is exactly the case this exists for), with two severities: **BLOCK** for a pattern on a line this change added, **REVIEW** for a pre-existing hit in a file you touched. That split is the whole reason the gate is usable: `--all` over the repo reports 101 BLOCK and 1060 REVIEW, and a gate that is red on arrival is a gate everyone learns to ignore. Beyond the greppable rules it does three things a regex alone cannot: it resolves each new `mcp/tools/*.kt` tool name and checks `McpToolPermissions` **LISTING and CALLING separately** (counting names file-wide conflates "listed twice in LISTING" with "listed once in each", and CALLING is additionally fed by a fold over `ToolCategories.CATEGORY_PERMISSIONS`, so checking one file reported 40 of 87 tools as unregistered); it requires an `McpToolGuards` call or an equivalent `context.isAdmin` check, because a missing CALLING entry fails **closed** and looks like a bug someone will chase while a missing guard fails **open** and looks like nothing; and file-context rules (XXE block, upload validation, archive traversal) emit BLOCK only when *this* change introduced the trigger. **Precision was tuned against the real corpus rather than guessed**: the first draft reported 269 BLOCK, of which most were false. "String contains SQL keywords" matches `"Failed to send test email from account: $id"`, so injection rules now require a query-construction context (`@Query(`/`createQuery(`/`nativeQuery`/a string *starting* with SELECT) **and** an interpolation — 24 findings to 1. Naming a secret in a log message is fine (`"using the default password is insecure"`) while logging its *value* is not, so the A09 rule looks for the value reaching the call — `$password`, or a `…Password`/`…Token` identifier passed as an argument — not for the word: 119 to 6, with `len(token)` and `…Configured` explicitly excluded. `A02-secret-lit` no longer fires on `DB_PASSWORD="REDACTED"` (value starting with `$`), and `A08-upload` triggers on a `: CompletedFileUpload` parameter rather than a vestigial import. **`scripts/test/owasp-check-test.sh` is the reason any of that can be trusted.** A static gate fails in two directions and only one is visible: a false positive is loud and gets fixed, a false negative is silent — the rule quietly stops matching and the gate reports OK forever. So the self-test builds a throwaway git repo, plants a deliberately vulnerable fixture per rule, asserts the rule fires **at the right severity**, then plants the repo's *approved* pattern for the same risk (bound `:param`, `DOMPurify.sanitize`, the four XXE `setFeature` calls, `BCryptPasswordEncoder`, a logged `tokenConfigured` boolean) and asserts it stays silent — 30 assertions, all green. It has already earned its keep twice: it caught `\b` in a `file_rule` trigger, which awk does not support, silently downgrading **every** BLOCK to REVIEW and turning the gate green (portable-ERE-only is now documented at the helper), and dogfooding the gate on this very change caught it flagging its own fixtures. Fixed with an exemption that is exactly two paths — `scripts/owasp-check.sh` (it contains the patterns it hunts) and `scripts/test/owasp-check-test.sh` (it is *made of* vulnerable fixtures) — deliberately **not** "tests are exempt", since `CLAUDE.md` forbids a literal credential in "source, tests, scripts or fixtures"; the self-test asserts an ordinary test file still fires, and the exempt paths are printed on every run so the blind spot is visible rather than assumed. **Wiring**: `CLAUDE.md`'s review gate now names the command and the BLOCK/REVIEW contract; `/testsuite` runs the self-test in its fast tier (step 5, "Skill sync and the OWASP gate"); skill registered in both harness trees plus `docs/SKILLS.md`, `docs/SKILLS_AND_AGENTS.md` and `AGENTS.md` (eleven skills → twelve). **Pre-existing findings surfaced by the first audit and left unfixed deliberately** — each encodes a decision that is not this change's to make: `MemoryController` is the only controller with no `@Secured` anywhere (it serves `GET /memory`); 37 MCP tools are in `LISTING` but absent from `CALLING`, including `add_requirement`, `create_release` and `compare_releases`, which per `CLAUDE.md`'s stated rule denies `tools/call` for delegated callers, though the API-key path in `McpToolPermissionService.hasPermission` may still reach them, so the real question is whether the two-map rule or the code is authoritative; `application_register` is absent from both (already documented as intentional); and `WorkgroupAccountsModal.tsx`/`WorkgroupDomainsModal.tsx` still read `localStorage.getItem('authToken')`, dead since the JWT moved to the HttpOnly cookie but exactly the A02 anti-pattern. **OWASP: no category touched** — the change adds two offline shell scripts and Markdown, no endpoint, entity, query or data path; both new scripts are dev tooling that nothing at runtime imports. **Not verified in this environment**: `pass-cli` is unavailable and `SECMAN_HOST` is unset, so the Principle 7 gates (`/e2ejs`, `/e2evulnexception`) did not run; `./gradlew build` and `./scripts/startbackenddev.sh` (Principle 5) were not run either, as no Kotlin, TypeScript or configuration file was changed. `./scripts/check-skill-sync.sh`, `./scripts/test/owasp-check-test.sh` (30/30) and `./scripts/owasp-check.sh` on this branch all pass.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:55:- **AWS account risk assessment: validation pass, three defects closed** — a review of the opt-in auto-start path (`manage-user-mappings import --start-risk-assessment --risk-usecase <name>`, mirrored on `import-s3`, REST `POST /api/user-mappings/bulk` and MCP `import_user_mappings`) confirmed the contract holds — the flag is off by default, the use case comes from a flag, and without the flag the import runs exactly as before — and turned up three things that did not. **(1) The deadline had no upper bound.** `validateStartRequest` rejected `< 1` and nothing else, so `--risk-deadline-days 2147483647` produced an `endDate` outside the SQL `DATE` range; because assessments are started *after* the mapping import commits, that surfaced as a per-account error with the mappings already persisted, and a merely absurd value like `100000` (one keystroke from `1000`) was accepted silently into an assessment the reminder scheduler — which looks two days ahead — would never wake up for. Now `MAX_DEADLINE_DAYS = 3650`, checked in `validateStartRequest` so REST and MCP share it, mirrored as `UserMappingCliService.MAX_RISK_DEADLINE_DAYS` in both CLI commands (the CLI is a separate Gradle module and cannot reference the backend constant; `ImportCommandTest` pins the two together), and clamped rather than thrown in `startAssessmentsForNewAccounts` for a direct service call, since that runs past the commit point. The MCP input schema now advertises `maximum`. **(2) The idempotent skip was reported as a failure.** When a pair already had an open assessment, `createAssessment` returned "an open risk assessment (id=…) already exists" in `AccountRiskAssessmentInfo.error`, so both CLI commands printed it as ❌/FAILED, counted it in `riskAssessmentFailures` and exited 1 — for an outcome that is the feature working correctly. The DTO gained `skipped` / `skipReason` (and the MCP result the same two fields), `error` stays null, and both CLIs render it as a skip that does not affect the exit code. **Load-bearing detail:** the owner-notification gate used to rely on `error != null` to suppress the duplicate mail, so it now tests `!info.skipped` as well — otherwise every re-import would re-notify. The path is only reachable when the mapping row was deleted and the account is imported again while its assessment is still open; a plain re-import never reaches the guard, because the account is no longer new. **(3) The email boundary was too loose.** `UserMappingService.emailRegex` was `^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$`, and `[^@]` matches control characters, spaces and commas — so `alice\r\nBcc: x@evil.com` passed validation. That address is not just a row: it becomes the SMTP recipient of the start and reminder mails, it is interpolated into log lines (`Started risk assessment … owner={}`), and it is written into the assessment's `notes`. The pattern now excludes whitespace and `, ; : < > " \` (a comma makes `InternetAddress.parse` split one recipient into two; a CR/LF reaches a log line), length is capped at the 255-char column width so an overlong address fails as one ordinary row error instead of a post-commit `DataException`, and the three "invalid …" messages that echo the rejected value run it through `sanitizeForMessage` (control characters → `?`, truncated at 80). The same pattern went into `UserMappingBulkImportService`'s `notifyAddress` copy and the CLI's `UserMappingValidator`. Also: `import-s3` now emits the "`--risk-usecase` is ignored because `--start-risk-assessment` is not set" warning `import` already had — silently ignoring it is how an operator ends up believing assessments ran. **Test skill.** `/aws-account-risk-assessment` (driver `scripts/test/test-e2e-aws-account-risk-assessment.sh`) gained three phases: the opt-in default (import a new account with no flag → mapping created, no assessment, no `AWS_ACCOUNT` asset; and the ignored-use-case warning), the deadline bound on both CLI and MCP, and a reworked idempotency phase that actually reaches the guard — it deletes the mapping so the account is new again while the assessment stays open, then asserts exit 0, a "skipped" line, no ❌, and still exactly one tracked assessment. Its **cleanup was also unsafe**: it deleted every risk assessment whose notes contained the substring `886` or `887`, which on a real environment means any assessment for a genuine AWS account whose id contains those digits. It now matches the owner-email prefix the service writes into the notes (`owner: e2e-awsra-`), which is both exact and stable across runs, sweeps mappings by that same prefix instead of this run's two timestamped ids (so earlier interrupted runs are cleaned up too), and finally removes the `AWS_ACCOUNT` basis assets — which nothing removed before, so every run leaked one. Accounts are now one per phase in a fixed `88[4-9]<stamp>000` shape, which is what the asset sweep matches. **Not verified in this session:** the environment had no Gradle distribution and no route to Maven Central, so the Kotlin changes are compile-unverified and neither the unit tests nor the E2E gates were run.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:56:- **Generic chat notifications (Slack + Telegram), configurable per user** — SecMan can now message a user in Slack and/or Telegram when a reportable event completes, with each user choosing their own destination and, independently per channel, which events they want. Two events ship: `CROWDSTRIKE_REPORT_COMPLETED` ("New CrowdStrike report completed") and `AWS_ACCOUNT_IMPORT_COMPLETED` ("New AWS account import completed"). **Architecture is transport- and event-agnostic on purpose.** Publishers know nothing about chat: they publish a `ChatNotificationEvent` (event type, title, summary, label/value fields) and `ChatNotificationEventListener` (`@EventListener @Async`) hands it to `ChatNotificationService`, which resolves subscribers, destinations and rendering. Adding a reportable event is a `NotificationEventType` constant plus one publish call — the settings APIs, both settings UIs and the dispatcher all derive from the enum, so nothing else changes. Adding a transport is one client plus one branch, with no publisher touched. **Subscriptions are rows, not columns**: `user_notification_subscription (user_id, channel, event_type)` — so a new event type or a whole new channel costs no migration, "who wants X over Slack" is a single indexed lookup on the dispatch path, and one user can route CrowdStrike to Slack and AWS imports to Telegram. Saving one channel's settings never disturbs the other's subscriptions (the replace is a per-channel diff, which also preserves `created_at` on kept rows). **Destination resolution.** Slack: personal incoming webhook → the user's channel via the workspace bot → the workspace default channel. Telegram: the user's chat ID is always required (Telegram addresses a conversation, not a person), with the token being the user's personal bot if set, otherwise the workspace bot — so a personal bot keeps working even when workspace delivery is switched off. A subscriber who is enabled but has nowhere to send is recorded as `SKIPPED`, not `FAILED`; the UI resolves the same precedence client-side (`resolveSlackDestination` / `resolveTelegramDestination`) and warns *before* save rather than letting someone tick boxes that silently deliver nothing. **Where the events fire.** AWS account imports complete in one call, so `UserMappingBulkImportService.execute` (REST bulk + MCP, tagged with the calling entry point) and both `ImportController` upload paths publish immediately, after the import has committed and last among the post-commit side effects. CrowdStrike has no such point: a full CLI import arrives as ~94 sub-batch requests across 3 concurrent workers with no well-defined last batch, so `ImportCompletionNotifier` accumulates the run's totals in memory and a `@Scheduled` sweep publishes exactly **one** event once `SECMAN_CHAT_CROWDSTRIKE_QUIET_PERIOD_SECONDS` (180s) have passed with no activity — the same server-side debounce shape, and for the same reason, as `MaterializedViewRefreshService.requestDeferredRefresh`, and it keeps working for older CLI versions, the `/api/crowdstrike/vulnerabilities/save` path and manual callers. **Security.** The per-user Slack webhook URL is the only place in the platform where a non-admin supplies a URL the backend then fetches, so it is checked against a fixed `https://hooks.slack.com/` prefix *and* parsed-host equality (a prefix match alone passes `https://hooks.slack.com.evil.example/...`), rejects userinfo, non-default ports and non-https, and redirects are never followed. The Telegram bot token is interpolated into the request URL **path** (`/bot<token>/sendMessage`), so its `<digits>:<secret>` shape is validated as a security control — a token containing `/` or `..` would otherwise redirect the request to another path on the API host. Slack channels and Telegram chat IDs are validated against conservative character classes. Every credential (both workspace bot tokens, each user's webhook URL and personal bot token) is stored through `EncryptedStringConverter`, never returned by any API — the responses report only `…Configured: true/false` — and the `***HIDDEN***` mask is accepted back to mean "keep the stored value", with `''` meaning "clear it". Slack messages escape Slack's three reserved characters so an imported hostname cannot inject a fake link; Telegram messages are sent with **no** `parse_mode`, deliberately, because MarkdownV2 reserves 18 characters and rejects the whole message on one unescaped occurrence. Every route acts on the caller's own settings — the user id comes from the token and is never read from the body. Dispatch is deliberately **not** `@Transactional`: it performs outbound HTTP with a multi-second timeout per recipient, and wrapping it would pin a pooled DB connection for the whole fan-out (the 2026-07-21 HikariCP starvation incident was exactly that shape). Delivery is per-recipient and per-channel isolated: one bad webhook never stops another user's message, one channel's outage never suppresses the other, and nothing can propagate back into the import that published the event. **New endpoints**: `GET /api/notification-events` (catalogue, authenticated); `GET/PUT /api/slack/settings`, `POST /api/slack/settings/test`, `GET/PUT /api/telegram/settings`, `POST /api/telegram/settings/test` (authenticated, self-scoped); `GET/PUT /api/slack/config`, `POST /api/slack/config/test`, `GET/PUT /api/telegram/config` (ADMIN). No Telegram workspace test endpoint — a bot token addresses no conversation on its own, so a meaningful test needs a chat ID and lives on the user page. **UI**: `/chat-notifications` (all users, linked from the account dropdown) with independent Slack and Telegram cards sharing a `NotificationEventSelector` and `ChatDeliveryStatusLine`; `/admin/chat-config` (ADMIN, linked under System Configuration). **Schema**: `V252__chat_notifications.sql` adds `slack_config`, `telegram_config`, `user_slack_settings`, `user_telegram_settings`, `user_notification_subscription`. **Tests**: `SlackClientTest` and `TelegramClientTest` (the URL/token/channel/chat-id allowlists, including that a rejected value never reaches the network), `ChatMessageRendererTest` (both flavours + Slack escaping), `ChatNotificationServiceTest` (24 cases: subscription filtering, both destination precedence chains, skipped-vs-failed, per-recipient and per-channel isolation, outcome recording), `ImportCompletionNotifierTest` (94 sub-batches → one event with correct totals, nothing published mid-import, totals reset between runs, the account-ID list cap), and `chatValidation.test.ts` on the frontend (17 cases mirroring the backend validators and both destination resolvers). On merging main, the newly-binding §OWASP Top 10 section prompted a re-read of the diff against A01–A10 and turned up one real gap: provider exception text was logged and persisted into `last_delivery_error` verbatim, and several JDK `HttpClient` exceptions echo the request URI — which for Telegram *contains the bot token* and for a Slack webhook *is* the credential. Both clients now scrub the secret out of any error before it is logged or stored (A02: no credential may reach a value that lands in a log), covered by a test per client. Migration renumbered `V251` → `V252__chat_notifications.sql`, since main landed its own `V251__user_profile_picture.sql` — two files sharing a Flyway version fails the migration at boot. **OWASP: A01/A02/A03/A04/A05/A08/A09/A10 touched — clean.** **Not verified in this environment**: `./gradlew build` and `./scripts/startbackenddev.sh` could not run — the session's egress policy blocks `services.gradle.org` and `repo1.maven.org`, and no Gradle 9.7.0 distribution or dependency cache is present — so the backend is compile-unverified and CLAUDE.md principle 5 and the principle-7 E2E gates are undischarged. The frontend gates did run: `npm ci && npm run build` clean, `npm test` 76 passing, and `@astrojs/check` reports zero type errors in any new or changed file (the 10 it finds are all pre-existing in untouched files).
docs/CHANGELOG.md:58:- **Profile picture management (upload / crop / replace / remove)** — any authenticated user can now set an avatar from `/profile`; it replaces the generic `bi-person-circle` icon beside their name in the header dropdown. Scope is deliberately **own picture only** — there are no ADMIN-manages-others endpoints, and none of the three routes (`GET`/`POST`/`DELETE /api/users/profile/picture`, all on the existing `UserProfileController`) takes a user identifier, so the subject is always `authentication.name` and cross-user access is *structurally* impossible rather than merely checked. The paths are two literal segments, so they cannot collide with the ADMIN-gated single-segment `@Get("/{id}")` on `UserController`, which shares the `/api/users` prefix. **Bytes are stored in the database but never as uploaded**: `ProfilePictureService` validates cheapest-first (size cap → MIME allowlist → filename-extension/MIME agreement → magic bytes → header-only dimensions → the `ImageReader`'s own `formatName`) and then decodes, centre-crops to a square, scales to 256 px and re-encodes. That round trip — not the magic-byte sniff — is the control that actually matters: it destroys polyglot payloads (a valid PNG with `<script>` appended still decodes as a PNG and would pass any header check) and strips EXIF/GPS metadata, verified by a dedicated test. The **dimension probe runs before `reader.read(0)`**, so a 2 MB PNG cannot decode into a multi-gigabyte `BufferedImage` and trip `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` on the 1 GB heap; without that guard the endpoint would be a single-request kill switch. WEBP is deliberately **absent** from the allowlist (the JDK has no WEBP reader, so accepting it would mean storing bytes that were never decoded) — this costs nothing in practice because the frontend cropper exports its canvas as PNG, so WEBP/HEIC sources still work end to end. SVG is rejected three independent ways: not in the allowlist, `.svg` already in `SecurityService.DANGEROUS_EXTENSIONS`, and no SVG `ImageReader` exists. Only the JDK is used (`javax.imageio`/`java.awt.image`); `-Djava.awt.headless=true` was pinned in `applicationDefaultJvmArgs`. Storage is a **side table** `user_profile_picture` (V251, 1:1, `ON DELETE CASCADE`), not a column on `users`: `users` is loaded on every authenticated request and **`@Basic(fetch = LAZY)` on a `@Lob` is inert without Hibernate bytecode enhancement, which this build does not enable** — a blob column on `users` would therefore be fetched eagerly, every time. For the same reason the hot metadata paths use the blob-free projection `findUpdatedAtByUserId`, never `findByUserId`. `UserProfileDto` and `AuthController.StatusResponse` gained `hasProfilePicture` + `profilePictureUpdatedAt` (both defaulted, so purely additive); `LoginResponse` and the four `sessionStorage['user']` writers were deliberately **left alone** — `auth-init.ts` and `login/success.astro` store the whole `/api/auth/status` response verbatim and `Login.tsx` redirects immediately into a fresh status call, so they pick the fields up for free. **The header `<img>` is gated on `hasProfilePicture` rather than rendered unconditionally with an `onError` fallback**: `tests/js-error-scanner.mjs` records any status ≥ 400 as a failure, so an unconditional request would 404 on every page for every user without a picture and fail the `/e2ejs` merge gate. For the same reason `DELETE` returns 204 unconditionally instead of 404 when nothing is set. Frontend: new `ProfilePictureCard.tsx` (preview, drag & drop, and a hand-rolled canvas crop/zoom step — pointer-drag to pan, wheel/slider to zoom, exported at 512 px via `canvas.toBlob`; no cropping library added, the repo carries none), mounted as the first card on `/profile` and seeded from the profile fetch that already ran, so no extra metadata request. After a save or removal it patches `window.currentUser`/`sessionStorage` and re-dispatches the **existing** `userLoaded` event that `Header.tsx` already listens for, so the navbar avatar updates without a reload. Serving uses `inline` disposition — the first such endpoint in the repo — which is safe only because the `Content-Type` served is the stored, service-chosen value and never the client's declared one, and the `Content-Disposition` filename is synthesized from a `Long` and a constant so no user input reaches a response header. Upload, removal **and rejection** are audit-logged (a stream of `PROFILE_PICTURE_UPLOAD_REJECTED` is exactly the signal wanted when someone probes with polyglots). Tests: `ProfilePictureServiceTest` (19 cases incl. the polyglot-stripping and bomb-guard proofs), `UserProfilePictureIntegrationTest` (happy path, replace-updates-one-row, every rejection branch, 401 on all three routes, idempotent delete, cross-user isolation, cascade). Docs: `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md` (`SECMAN_PROFILE_PICTURE_*`).

# Changelog (archived from CLAUDE.md)

## Context summaries preserved before compression (2026-09-06)

- **Source-review quick wins: hot-path queries, transaction scope, dashboard parallelism (2026-08-27)** — first execution pass over `docs/SOURCE_REVIEW_COMPLEXITY_SPEED.md` §6. `AssetFilterService` admin paths use a new `findAllIds()` projection and the scan path became two batch queries (no more full-table `findAll()` + in-memory filter); eight `findAll().filter{hasRole}` sites became role queries; `NormMappingService` no longer holds a transaction across its OpenRouter loop (per-requirement apply transactions via self-`Provider`); the private CrowdStrike deadlock-retry copy merged into shared `DeadlockRetry`; new `GET /api/workgroups/tree` replaces the frontend's recursive per-node walk; home dashboard fetches run concurrently, the `McpDashboard` interval leak is fixed, dead `utils/api-config.ts` and the legacy unpaged `getCurrentVulnerabilities` are deleted. Backend build/startup + E2E gates still owed before merge (authoring env had no Gradle mirror/DB/pass-cli) — detail in `docs/CHANGELOG.md`.

- **AWS account display names link accounts to workgroups (2026-08-25)** — an account whose `display_name` is `DevOps-x` now belongs to workgroup **`aws-DevOps-x`**: matched exactly (case-insensitively) on the `aws-` prefix, **created** when missing. One implementation, `WorkgroupAccountLinkService`, reached from the import (CLI/REST/MCP `displayName`, after the mappings commit) and from a correction path that re-links from stored names with no file — CLI `manage-user-mappings link-workgroups`, `POST /api/user-mappings/link-workgroup-accounts`, MCP `link_workgroup_aws_accounts`. The name is persisted as `user_mapping.aws_account_name` (V260) and deliberately kept **out** of the unique key. A display name that cannot be a workgroup name is an error row, never a forced creation; already-linked accounts are idempotent no-ops. Also fixed: six workgroup MCP tools were in `LISTING` but not `.CALLING` (listed yet uncallable). `docs/AWS_ACCOUNT_WORKGROUP_LINKING.md`.

- **Full `excepted` recompute chunked to stop multi-minute lock holds (2026-08-24)** — `recomputeExceptedAll()` was one `UPDATE` with **no WHERE**, locking every `vulnerability` row (~1.8M) plus `vulnerability_exception` for 53-180s, so every concurrent writer (bulk exception delete/import, CrowdStrike import, per-asset recompute) queued behind it. `AsyncExceptionRecompute.recomputeAllChunked` now drives bounded **keyset** chunks (`CHUNK_SIZE` 10,000) through `recomputeExceptedForIdRange`, each its own REQUIRES_NEW transaction with per-chunk `DeadlockRetry`. Atomicity is deliberately given up (the path is already `@Async` and eventual); a failure now leaves a converged prefix. `recomputeExceptedAll()` is retained for integration tests only. `docs/CHANGELOG.md`.

## Full change entries

The full history. Every change is written here **verbatim** when it happens; CLAUDE.md's `## Recent Changes` carries a 2–3 line summary of the three newest and nothing more. Nothing is ever summarized on the way in — this file is the greppable detail. Newest first.

- **External web exposure and software-component inventory (2026-09-19)** — `extensions/secman_web_check` now derives a best-effort inventory from evidence the bounded HTTP collector already retrieved: conservative script and stylesheet URL signatures identify selected JavaScript/CSS libraries, and normalized `Server` signatures identify web servers. Detection never crawls or fetches a cross-origin resource merely to fingerprint it, and persisted/uploaded inventory stores no response body, cookie, credential, raw header value, URL query, or fragment. Each result carries an external-exposure observation explicitly tied to the `secman-web-check` vantage point; a failed or policy-denied collection stays `UNKNOWN` rather than claiming the site is down. Components and exposure now render in terminal, JSON schema 1.1, and the self-contained HTML report; MariaDB schema v2 adds exposure fields plus parameterized `scan_component` rows and component counts. `--targets-from-secman` reads the selected scanner's authorized integration subjects, skips subjects without a URI, retains exact subject/asset IDs, and uses that binding on upload instead of rematching a hostname; positional, text-file, and AWS CSV target modes remain available and mutually exclusive. The additive integration-run v1 `inventory` object is accepted only for `WEB_SECURITY`, validated at 500 components, hashed into retry identity, and stored immutably on the run. Current `web_exposure` and `web_component` rows update in the same transaction as findings; missing components resolve only after a newer successful inventory snapshot marked complete, independent of finding coverage. Asset-scoped REST adds `/api/integrations/v1/web-exposure/summary`, `/web-exposures`, and `/web-components`; MCP adds `get_web_exposure_summary`, `list_web_exposures`, and `list_web_components` in both permission maps with delegation, `INTEGRATIONS_READ`, and an ADMIN/VULN/SECCHAMPION guard. The same roles see **Analytics → External exposure**, with summary KPIs and paged asset/component tables. REST and MCP deliberately reuse one service; no SOAP adapter was added because SecMan has no SOAP consumer or reusable SOAP authentication/authorization boundary. Component inventory is not a vulnerability and is not written to `installed_product`; existing `WEB_SECURITY` findings still project under the generic `Webserver` product. Tests cover detection/redaction, reporting, local persistence, SecMan payload/direct binding, validation, atomic component lifecycle, MCP permissions/roles, and UI presentation.

- **Catch-all workgroup safety and direct workgroup links (2026-09-17)** — application settings now expose a direct-user threshold for catch-all workgroups, defaulting to 100. Existing qualifying workgroups are disabled by migration, saving a new threshold immediately disables newly qualifying groups, and user-assignment/config-import paths re-check affected memberships server-side. The rule is fail-closed but never auto-enables a group after membership drops; an administrator must deliberately re-enable it. Disabled workgroups already grant no effective asset/account/domain access, and every automatic disable invalidates the workgroup-access cache and records actor, target, user count, threshold, and outcome. User Management workgroup badges now link to `/workgroups?workgroupId=…`, which opens the existing tree detail panel for that exact group. The workgroup table also uses WebKit-safe sticky header cells so Safari scrolling no longer paints rows through the header.

- **CrowdStrike imports include domain controllers (2026-09-17)** — Falcon reports domain controllers under the separate exact `product_type_desc = 'Domain Controller'` category, so the production vulnerability and installed-product imports previously omitted them while querying only `Server`. The shared client now exposes `DOMAIN_CONTROLLER` and the composite `SERVER_FAMILY` scope; composite scopes issue bounded queries for each exact Falcon category and deduplicate agent IDs before the existing vulnerability pipeline runs. `ALL` now means Server + Domain Controller + Workstation. `scripts/import.sh`, `scripts/importaws.sh`, and `scripts/importproducts.sh` use `SERVER_FAMILY`, and the main import uses the documented 30-day last-seen window. Domain controllers deliberately persist as SecMan `SERVER` assets, retaining existing access, risk, KPI, notification, identity-conflict, and reconciliation behavior with no schema migration. Focused tests pin enum expansion, exact FQL filters, recency propagation, AID deduplication, and Discover product coverage.

- **Web findings identify as findings and group under Webserver (2026-09-17)** — the current-vulnerabilities table now labels its identifier column **CVE/Finding**, reflecting that integration projections use stable finding identities rather than CVE identifiers. New `WEB_SECURITY` findings project `Webserver` into the Product field instead of exposing their internal external IDs there; V266 backfills both active vulnerability projections and the durable `integration_finding.projection_product` used when resolved findings reopen. The change is deliberately source-scoped: `VISUAL`, `GITHUB_AI`, CrowdStrike and manual vulnerabilities retain their existing product values, while the stable `INT:...` projection key remains unchanged for per-finding identity and exceptions. - **Source-review quick wins: hot-path queries, transaction scope, dashboard parallelism (2026-08-27)** — first execution pass over `docs/SOURCE_REVIEW_COMPLEXITY_SPEED.md` §6 (Phases 1–2). **Access-path queries**: the ADMIN/SECCHAMPION short-circuits in `AssetFilterService` now use a new `AssetRepository.findAllIds()` projection instead of materializing the whole asset table twice per request just to extract ids; the non-admin scan path replaced `scanRepository.findAll()` + in-memory uploader filtering (and a per-workgroup user-query loop) with two batch queries, `UserRepository.findByWorkgroupsIdInOrderByUsernameAsc` and `ScanRepository.findByUploadedByInOrderByScanDateDesc` — same predicate, same result set, no full-table scan. - **Full `excepted` recompute chunked to stop multi-minute lock holds (2026-08-24)** — `VulnerabilityRepository.recomputeExceptedAll()` was a single `UPDATE vulnerability v JOIN asset a … SET v.excepted = CASE WHEN EXISTS(…)` **with no WHERE clause**. It took exclusive row locks on every `vulnerability` row (~1.8M in production) and, through its correlated subquery, read locks on `vulnerability_exception` — holding both for the entire 53–180s transaction. Every concurrent writer to either table then blocked until lock-wait-timeout: bulk exception delete/import, CrowdStrike imports, per-asset recomputes. `DeadlockRetry` absorbed the failure, which is exactly why it stayed hidden — but the *other* operation still paid the full timeout first, observed as ~40s per `delete_all_vulnerability_exceptions` in both E2E runs, contending with "Async full excepted recompute complete: 1824736 rows in 53481 ms". Fix: `AsyncExceptionRecompute.recomputeAllChunked` drives the recompute as bounded **keyset** chunks (`CHUNK_SIZE` 10,000) through the new `recomputeExceptedForIdRange(afterId, throughId)`, each in its own REQUIRES_NEW transaction with per-chunk `DeadlockRetry`. Lock hold per transaction drops from minutes to milliseconds, so competing writers interleave between chunks instead of queueing behind one lock set; a chunk that loses a race replays only its own id range instead of the w…64856 tokens truncated…_statistics_cache` under `cache_key = "edr_coverage_kpi"` — no new table). "EC2 instance" = non-blank `cloudInstanceId` (same fence as `countAllAwsAssetsWithInstanceId`). **"Has CrowdStrike" deliberately does NOT use `crowdstrike_last_imported_at`**: `scripts/import.sh` filters `--severity CRITICAL,HIGH` and `CrowdStrikeApiClientImpl` drops empty batches, so a fully-patched host with a healthy sensor never sets it and a KPI built on it would punish good hygiene. New column `asset.crowdstrike_agent_seen_at` (V248) is instead stamped from the import's **Stage-1 queried-host population** — already transmitted to `POST /api/crowdstrike/servers/reconcile-stale` as `queriedHosts` and already resolved to assets there, previously discarded. Stamping happens *before* the zero-refresh brake (an aborted sweep is still valid agent evidence) and no-ops on empty `queriedHosts` (preserving the sweep's fail-safe); the deferred-refresh trigger became `deleted > 0 || stamped > 0` so a clean run still refreshes the KPI. **No CLI or shared-client change was needed.** Numerator requires a sighting within `AGENT_SEEN_FRESHNESS_DAYS = 7` so the metric tracks *current* coverage; `available=false` (card reads "Not available") until at least one asset has ever been stamped, so a fresh deploy does not report a false 0%.

Detection never crawls or fetches a cross-origin resource merely to fingerprint it, and persisted/uploaded inventory stores no response body, cookie, credential, raw header value, URL query, or fragment. Each result carries an external-exposure observation explicitly tied to the `secman-web-check` vantage point; a failed or policy-denied collection stays `UNKNOWN` rather than claiming the site is down. Components and exposure now render in terminal, JSON schema 1.1, and the self-contained HTML report; MariaDB schema v2 adds exposure fields plus parameterized `scan_component` rows and component counts. `--targets-from-secman` reads the selected scanner's authorized integration subjects, skips subjects without a URI, retains exact subject/asset IDs, and uses that binding on upload instead of rematching a hostname; positional, text-file, and AWS CSV target modes remain available and mutually exclusive. The additive integration-run v1 `inventory` object is accepted only for `WEB_SECURITY`, validated at 500 components, hashed into retry identity, and stored immutably on the run. Current `web_exposure` and `web_component` rows update in the same transaction as findings; missing components resolve only after a newer successful inventory snapshot marked complete, independent of finding coverage. Asset-scoped REST adds `/api/integrations/v1/web-exposure/summary`, `/web-exposures`, and `/web-components`; MCP adds `get_web_exposure_summary`, `list_web_exposures`, and `list_web_components` in both permission maps with delegation, `INTEGRATIONS_READ`, and an ADMIN/VULN/SECCHAMPION guard. Existing qualifying workgroups are disabled by migration, saving a new threshold immediately disables newly qualifying groups, and user-assignment/config-import paths re-check affected memberships server-side. The rule is fail-closed but never auto-enables a group after membership drops; an administrator must deliberately re-enable it. Per (new account, owner email) pair: an `AWS_ACCOUNT` asset (`AWS Account <id>`, `cloudAccountId` set, owner = email) is found-or-created, an ASSET-based `RiskAssessment` (status STARTED, endDate = today + deadline, respondent = owner user when one exists) is created **after** the import commits, and the owner is emailed. **Reminders 2 days and 1 day before the deadline** are sent by `AwsAccountRiskAssessmentReminderScheduler` (daily 08:15) to the owner; sent-state persists on the new `aws_account_risk_assessment` table (V237, `AwsAccountRiskAssessment` entity) so each reminder fires exactly once and only import-created assessments are reminded (missed 2-day reminders collapse into the 1-day send). import io.micronaut.http.cookie.Cookie
import io.micronaut.http.cookie.SameSite
import jakarta.inject.Singleton
import java.time.Duration

/**
 * Service for creating authentication cookies.
 *
 * Provides consistent cookie creation for both local login (AuthController)
 * and OAuth login (OAuthController) to ensure the same HttpOnly secure cookie
 * is used across all authentication methods.
 */
@Singleton
class AuthCookieService(
    @io.micronaut.context.annotation.Value("\${secman.auth.cookie-secure:true}")
    private val cookieSecure: Boolean
) {
    companion object {
        const val AUTH_COOKIE_NAME = "secman_auth"
        private val AUTH_COOKIE_MAX_AGE = Duration.ofHours(8)
    }

    /**
     * Create HttpOnly secure cookie for JWT token.
     * Security properties:
     * - HttpOnly: Prevents JavaScript access (XSS protection)
     * - Secure: Only sent over HTTPS (configurable for development)
     * - SameSite=Lax: CSRF protection while allowing navigation
     * - Path=/: Available for all API endpoints
     *
     * Note: Set SECMAN_AUTH_COOKIE_SECURE=false for local development over HTTP
     */
    fun createAuthCookie(token: String): Cookie {
        return Cookie.of(AUTH_COOKIE_NAME, token)
            .httpOnly(true)
            .secure(cookieSecure)
            .sameSite(SameSite.Lax)
            .maxAge(AUTH_COOKIE_MAX_AGE)
            .path("/")
    }

    /**
     * Create expired cookie to clear authentication.
     */
    fun createLogoutCookie(): Cookie {
        return Cookie.of(AUTH_COOKIE_NAME, "")
            .httpOnly(true)
            .secure(cookieSecure)
            .sameSite(SameSite.Lax)
            .maxAge(Duration.ZERO)
            .path("/")
    }
}

/**
         * The role gate for each section, and the single most important table
         * in this file.
         *
         * Each entry mirrors the `@Secured` annotation on the secman controller
         * the data comes from, so a user sees on their phone exactly the
         * sections they could open in the web UI — no more, and no less:
         *
         *  - [SECTION_KPIS]       DashboardController        @Secured("ADMIN","SECCHAMPION")
         *  - [SECTION_EXCEPTIONS] VulnerabilityExceptionRequestController
         *                         .getPendingCount           @Secured("ADMIN","SECCHAMPION")
         *  - [SECTION_IMPORTS]    CrowdStrikeController      ADMIN/VULN
         *  - the remaining three are the admin summary, which is ADMIN-only.
         *
         * **When you change a controller's `@Secured`, change the matching row
         * here.** Nothing in the build can catch the drift: the relay will
         * happily enforce whatever it is told, and the result is a phone
         * showing data the web UI would refuse. `RelaySnapshotBuilderTest`
         * pins the pairs that exist today.
         */
        val SECTION_POLICIES: Map<String, RelaySectionPolicy> = mapOf(
            SECTION_TOTALS to RelaySectionPolicy(
                requiredRoles = listOf("ADMIN"),
                description = "Asset, vulnerability and user counts"
            ),
            SECTION_KPIS to RelaySectionPolicy(
                requiredRoles = listOf("ADMIN", "SECCHAMPION"),
                description = "AWS clean-server and EDR coverage KPIs"
            ),
            SECTION_EXCEPTIONS to RelaySectionPolicy(
                requiredRoles = listOf("ADMIN", "SECCHAMPION"),
                description = "Vulnerability exception requests awaiting review"
            ),
            SECTION_IMPORTS to RelaySectionPolicy(
                requiredRoles = listOf("ADMIN", "VULN"),
                description = "Freshness of the last CrowdStrike import"
            ),
            SECTION_TOP_PRODUCTS to RelaySectionPolicy(
                requiredRoles = listOf("ADMIN"),
                description = "Products with the most vulnerabilities"
            ),
            SECTION_TOP_SERVERS to RelaySectionPolicy(
                requiredRoles = listOf("ADMIN"),
                description = "Servers with the most vulnerabilities"
            ),
            SECTION_INTEGRATIONS to RelaySectionPolicy(
                requiredRoles = listOf("ADMIN"),
                description = "Integration finding counts and scan coverage freshness"
            )
        )

        /** Renders an instant as the RFC 3339 UTC string the relay parses. */
        fun rfc3339(instant: Instant): String = DateTimeFormatter.ISO_INSTANT.format(instant)

        /**
         * Renders a zone-less [LocalDateTime] as an ISO local timestamp.
         *
         * Deliberately *not* stamped with a zone: these values come out of the
         * database as LocalDateTime with no recorded offset, and inventing UTC
         * would silently shift every displayed time by the server's offset. The
         * app renders them as "server local time", which is what they are.
            unavailable: .meansServerBusy
        )
        store(token: token)
        return token
    }

    // MARK: - Reads

    public func session() async throws -> RelaySession {
        try await send(path: "/api/v1/session", method: "GET", body: RelayClient.noBody, authenticated: true)
    }

    /// Freshness and entitlements without the payload — the cheap poll.
    public func meta() async throws -> RelayMeta {
        try await send(
            path: "/api/v1/meta", method: "GET", body: RelayClient.noBody,
            authenticated: true, unavailable: .meansNoSnapshot
        )
    }

    public func status() async throws -> RelaySnapshot {
        let snapshot: RelaySnapshot = try await send(
            path: "/api/v1/status", method: "GET", body: RelayClient.noBody,
            authenticated: true, unavailable: .meansNoSnapshot
        )
        guard snapshot.schemaVersion == relaySupportedSnapshotSchemaVersion else {
            // Refuse rather than render half of it: a status screen that
            // silently drops the field it did not understand is worse than one
            // that says "update the app".
            throw RelayError.unsupportedSchema(
                found: snapshot.schemaVersion,
                supported: relaySupportedSnapshotSchemaVersion
            )
        }
        return snapshot
    }

    /// The snapshot, or nil when the relay is healthy but secman has not pushed.
    ///
    /// "Waiting for secman" is a normal state on a freshly deployed relay, not
    /// a failure, and modelling it as one forces every caller to catch.
    public func statusIfAvailable() async throws -> RelaySnapshot? {
        do {
            return try await status()
        } catch RelayError.noSnapshotYet {
            return nil

+package com.secman.util
+
+/** Canonical cloud identifiers exposed by inventory list views. */
+object CloudIdentifierDisplay {
+    private val awsAccountId = Regex("^[0-9]{12}$")
+    private val ec2InstanceId = Regex("^i-(?:[0-9a-f]{8}|[0-9a-f]{17})$", RegexOption.IGNORE_CASE)
+
+    fun accountId(value: String?): String? = value?.trim()?.takeIf(awsAccountId::matches)
+
+    fun instanceId(value: String?): String? = value?.trim()?.takeIf(ec2InstanceId::matches)?.lowercase()
+}

+package com.secman.service
+
+import com.secman.domain.Asset
+import jakarta.inject.Singleton
+import jakarta.persistence.EntityManager
+
+/** Executes one bounded inventory query without initializing asset collections. */
+@Singleton
+open class AssetOverviewQueryService(private val entityManager: EntityManager) {
+    /** Optional filters accepted by the overview endpoint. */
+    data class Filters(
+        val name: String?,
+        val ipAddress: String?,
+        val owner: String?,
+        val adDomain: String?,
+        val accountId: String?,
+        val workgroupId: Long?
+    )
+
+    /** A page of assets plus the exact matching row count. */
+    data class Result(val assets: List<Asset>, val total: Long)
+
+    /** Applies access IDs before database pagination; null IDs mean a globally authorized caller. */
+    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
+    open fun search(ids: Set<Long>?, filters: Filters, page: Int, pageSize: Int): Result {
+        if (ids != null && ids.isEmpty()) return Result(emptyList(), 0)
+
+        val rows = entityManager.createNativeQuery(ROW_QUERY, Asset::class.java)
+        val count = entityManager.createNativeQuery(COUNT_QUERY)
+        bind(rows, ids, filters)
+        bind(count, ids, filters)
+        rows.firstResult = page * pageSize
+        rows.maxResults = pageSize
+        return Result(rows.resultList as List<Asset>, (count.singleResult as Number).toLong())
+    }
+
+    private fun bind(query: jakarta.persistence.Query, ids: Set<Long>?, filters: Filters) {
+        query.setParameter("restrictIds", ids != null)
+        query.setParameter("ids", ids ?: setOf(-1L))
+        query.setParameter("name", filters.name)
+        query.setParameter("ip", filters.ipAddress)
+        query.setParameter("owner", filters.owner)
+        query.setParameter("adDomain", filters.adDomain)
+        query.setParameter("accountId", filters.accountId)
+        query.setParameter("workgroupId", filters.workgroupId)
+    }
+
+    companion object {
+        private const val ROW_QUERY = """
+            SELECT a.* FROM asset a
+            WHERE (:restrictIds = FALSE OR a.id IN (:ids))
+              AND (:name IS NULL OR LOCATE(LOWER(:name), LOWER(a.name)) > 0)
+              AND (:ip IS NULL OR LOCATE(LOWER(:ip), LOWER(a.ip)) > 0)
+              AND (:owner IS NULL OR LOCATE(LOWER(:owner), LOWER(a.owner)) > 0)
+              AND (:adDomain IS NULL OR LOCATE(LOWER(:adDomain), LOWER(a.ad_domain)) > 0)
+              AND (:accountId IS NULL OR LOCATE(:accountId, a.cloud_account_id) > 0)
+              AND (:workgroupId IS NULL OR EXISTS (
+                  SELECT 1 FROM asset_workgroups aw
+                  JOIN workgroup w ON w.id = aw.workgroup_id
+                  WHERE aw.asset_id = a.id AND aw.workgroup_id = :workgroupId AND w.enabled = TRUE
+              ))
+            ORDER BY a.created_at DESC, a.id DESC
+        """
+        private const val COUNT_QUERY = """
+            SELECT COUNT(*) FROM asset a
+            WHERE (:restrictIds = FALSE OR a.id IN (:ids))
+              AND (:name IS NULL OR LOCATE(LOWER(:name), LOWER(a.name)) > 0)
+              AND (:ip IS NULL OR LOCATE(LOWER(:ip), LOWER(a.ip)) > 0)
+              AND (:owner IS NULL OR LOCATE(LOWER(:owner), LOWER(a.owner)) > 0)
+              AND (:adDomain IS NULL OR LOCATE(LOWER(:adDomain), LOWER(a.ad_domain)) > 0)
+              AND (:accountId IS NULL OR LOCATE(:accountId, a.cloud_account_id) > 0)
+              AND (:workgroupId IS NULL OR EXISTS (
+                  SELECT 1 FROM asset_workgroups aw
+                  JOIN workgroup w ON w.id = aw.workgroup_id
+                  WHERE aw.asset_id = a.id AND aw.workgroup_id = :workgroupId AND w.enabled = TRUE
+              ))
+        """
+    }
+}

@@ -0,0 +1,119 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Remove one explicitly retained manual fixture recorded by create-test-data.sh.
+set -euo pipefail
+
+REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)"
+MANIFEST_DIR="$REPO_ROOT/.e2e-logs/manual-fixtures"
+[[ $# -eq 1 ]] || { echo "Usage: $0 <fixture-manifest.json>" >&2; exit 2; }
+MANIFEST="$(realpath "$1")"
+[[ "$MANIFEST" == "$MANIFEST_DIR/"* && -f "$MANIFEST" ]] || {
+    echo "Manifest must be a recorded manual fixture under $MANIFEST_DIR" >&2; exit 2;
+}
+
+if [[ -z "${SECMAN_HOST_RESOLVED:-}" ]]; then
+    export SECMAN_HOST="pass://Test/SECMAN/SECMAN_HOST"
+    export SECMAN_ADMIN_NAME="pass://Test/SECMAN/SECMAN_ADMIN_NAME"
+    export SECMAN_ADMIN_PASS="pass://Test/SECMAN/SECMAN_ADMIN_PASS"
+    export SECMAN_USER_PASS="pass://Test/SECMAN/SECMAN_USER_PASS"
+    export SECMAN_HOST_RESOLVED=1
+    exec pass-cli run -- "$0" "$MANIFEST"
+fi
+
+for name in SECMAN_HOST SECMAN_ADMIN_NAME SECMAN_ADMIN_PASS SECMAN_USER_PASS; do
+    [[ -n "${!name:-}" ]] || { echo "Missing $name" >&2; exit 2; }
+done
+BASE_URL="$SECMAN_HOST"
+[[ "$BASE_URL" == http://* || "$BASE_URL" == https://* ]] || BASE_URL="https://$BASE_URL"
+BASE_URL="${BASE_URL%/}"
+
+target="$(jq -r '.target // empty' "$MANIFEST")"
+[[ "$target" == "$BASE_URL" ]] || {
+    echo "Fixture target differs from the current SecMan host; refusing cleanup" >&2; exit 2;
+}
+
+user_name="$(jq -r '.userName // empty' "$MANIFEST")"
+user_email="$(jq -r '.userEmail // empty' "$MANIFEST")"
+asset_name="$(jq -r '.assetName // empty' "$MANIFEST")"
+user_id="$(jq -r '.userId // empty' "$MANIFEST")"
+asset_id="$(jq -r '.assetId // empty' "$MANIFEST")"
+request_id="$(jq -r '.requestId // empty' "$MANIFEST")"
+[[ "$user_name" == testdata-user-* && "$asset_name" == testdata-host-* ]] || {
+    echo "Manifest lacks manual fixture identity" >&2; exit 2;
+}
+
+admin_jar="$(mktemp)"
+user_jar="$(mktemp)"
+response_file="$(mktemp)"
+trap 'rm -f "$admin_jar" "$user_jar" "$response_file"' EXIT
+
+login() {
+    local jar="$1" name="$2" password="$3" status
+    status="$(curl -sS -o "$response_file" -w '%{http_code}' -c "$jar" \
+        -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -X POST "$BASE_URL/api/auth/login" \
+        --data "$(jq -nc --arg u "$name" --arg p "$password" '{username:$u,password:$p}')")"
+    [[ "$status" == 200 ]] || { echo "Login failed (HTTP $status)" >&2; return 1; }
+}
+
+get_status() {
+    curl -sS -o "$response_file" -w '%{http_code}' -b "$1" "$BASE_URL$2"
+}
+
+delete_status() {
+    curl -sS -o "$response_file" -w '%{http_code}' -b "$1" -X DELETE "$BASE_URL$2"
+}
+
+login "$admin_jar" "$SECMAN_ADMIN_NAME" "$SECMAN_ADMIN_PASS"
+
+if [[ "$request_id" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
+    status="$(get_status "$admin_jar" "/api/vulnerability-exception-requests/$request_id")"
+    if [[ "$status" == 200 ]]; then
+        jq -e --argjson id "$request_id" --argjson user "$user_id" \
+            --argjson asset "$asset_id" --arg name "$user_name" \
+            '.id==$id and .requestedByUserId==$user and .assetId==$asset and .requestedByUsername==$name' \
+            "$response_file" >/dev/null || {
+                echo "Exception request identity mismatch; preserving it" >&2; exit 1;
+            }
+        login "$user_jar" "$user_name" "$SECMAN_USER_PASS"
+        status="$(delete_status "$user_jar" "/api/vulnerability-exception-requests/$request_id/delete")"
+        [[ "$status" == 204 ]] || { echo "Request cleanup failed (HTTP $status)" >&2; exit 1; }
+    elif [[ "$status" != 404 ]]; then
+        echo "Request lookup failed (HTTP $status)" >&2; exit 1
+    fi
+fi
+
+if [[ "$asset_id" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
+    status="$(get_status "$admin_jar" "/api/assets/$asset_id")"
+    if [[ "$status" == 200 ]]; then
+        jq -e --argjson id "$asset_id" --arg name "$asset_name" \
+            '.id==$id and .name==$name' "$response_file" >/dev/null || {
+                echo "Asset identity mismatch; preserving it" >&2; exit 1;
+            }
+        status="$(delete_status "$admin_jar" "/api/assets/$asset_id")"
+        [[ "$status" == 204 || "$status" == 200 ]] || {
+            echo "Asset cleanup failed (HTTP $status)" >&2; exit 1;
+        }
+    elif [[ "$status" != 404 ]]; then
+        echo "Asset lookup failed (HTTP $status)" >&2; exit 1
+    fi
+fi
+
+if [[ "$user_id" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
+    status="$(get_status "$admin_jar" "/api/users/$user_id")"
+    if [[ "$status" == 200 ]]; then
+        jq -e --argjson id "$user_id" --arg name "$user_name" --arg email "$user_email" \
+            '.id==$id and .username==$name and .email==$email' "$response_file" >/dev/null || {
+                echo "User identity mismatch; preserving it" >&2; exit 1;
+            }
+        status="$(delete_status "$admin_jar" "/api/users/$user_id")"
+        [[ "$status" == 204 || "$status" == 200 ]] || {
+            echo "User cleanup failed (HTTP $status)" >&2; exit 1;
+        }
+    elif [[ "$status" != 404 ]]; then
+        echo "User lookup failed (HTTP $status)" >&2; exit 1
+    fi
+fi
+
+temp="$(mktemp "$MANIFEST.XXXXXX")"
+jq --arg cleaned "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" '.cleanedAt=$cleaned' "$MANIFEST" > "$temp"
+mv "$temp" "$MANIFEST"
+echo "Manual fixture cleanup completed: $MANIFEST"

+# Source and call secman_test_require_isolated before database-mutating E2E work.
+secman_test_require_isolated() {
+    local expected_db="${SECMAN_TEST_ISOLATED_DB:-}" token="${SECMAN_TEST_OWNER_TOKEN:-}"
+    local actual_token
+    if [[ ! "$expected_db" =~ ^secman_e2e_[a-f0-9]{16}$ || ! "$token" =~ ^[a-f0-9]{32}$ ]]; then
+        echo "This test requires scripts/test/run-isolated-e2e.sh" >&2
+        return 2
+    fi
+    if [[ "${DB_NAME:-}" != "$expected_db" ||
+          "${DB_CONNECT:-}" != "jdbc:mariadb://127.0.0.1:3306/$expected_db" ||
+          "${BASE_URL:-}" != "${SECMAN_E2E_BACKEND_URL:-}" ||
+          "${SECMAN_E2E_BACKEND_URL:-}" != http://127.0.0.1:18080 ]]; then
+        echo "Test target does not match its disposable database and backend" >&2
+        return 2
+    fi
+    if [[ -z "${DB_USER:-}" || -z "${DB_PASS:-}" ]]; then
+        echo "Disposable database credentials are missing" >&2
+        return 2
+    fi
+    actual_token="$(MYSQL_PWD="REDACTED" mariadb --batch --skip-column-names \
+        -h 127.0.0.1 -u "$DB_USER" "$expected_db" \
+        -e 'SELECT owner_token FROM secman_e2e_owner LIMIT 1' 2>/dev/null)" || return 2
+    if [[ "$actual_token" != "$token" ]]; then
+        echo "Disposable database ownership marker does not match" >&2
+        return 2
+    fi
+}
